label: DC convergence aids
lesson:
# DC convergence aids

When plain Newton fails on an operating point, simulators fall back on a toolbox of convergence aids: junction limiting, damping, gmin stepping, source stepping, pseudo-transient continuation and user-supplied nodesets. Each aid attacks a different cause of failure and each has side effects. A tool designer chooses the order in which a simulator tries them; a user, or an agent, must diagnose which one a failing deck needs.

## Why Newton fails on circuits

Newton fails for identifiable reasons. A node with no DC path to ground, touching only capacitors or gates, has an empty row, so the matrix is singular. An exponential device evaluated at a large overshoot overflows or produces a useless Jacobian. Far from the solution, full Newton steps can cycle between two iterates. Circuits with positive feedback, such as latches, bandgaps and Schmitt triggers, have several DC solutions, and Newton may land on an unintended one or wander between their basins. A singular matrix points to topology; overflow to missing limiting; cycling to damping; an unexpected solution to the initial guess.

## Choosing an aid

Gmin stepping attaches a large conductance to ground at every node and shrinks it, making the start nearly linear. Source stepping ramps every independent source from zero, where the all-zero solution is exact, up to its full value. Pseudo-transient continuation adds artificial capacitance and integrates in time until the circuit settles, following a physical trajectory. A .nodeset gives Newton an initial guess at chosen nodes and is released after the first iterations, steering it toward the intended one of several solutions. For a bandgap that keeps landing in its zero-current state, a nodeset on the output near 1.2 V is the cleanest fix.

## What each aid costs and hides

Every aid has a price. Intermediate continuation solutions belong to a modified circuit and mean nothing until the final solve converges. Source stepping fails at a turning point, where the solution curve of a hysteretic circuit folds back, and needs arc-length continuation or pseudo-transient instead. A large global gmin set as an option stays in the circuit and corrupts high-impedance nodes. Aggressive damping turns quadratic convergence into slow linear creep: the answer is as accurate, but it costs many more factorizations. The safest fix changes the path to the solution, not the equations being solved.

## Going deeper

Najm, "Circuit Simulation" (Wiley, 2010), chapter 4; the Xyce Users' Guide, chapter on homotopy and convergence; the ngspice manual, section on convergence options.

problems.q:
An operating point oscillates between two iterates and never meets the tolerance. Which property of Newton explains this?

A) Newton converges only locally; far from a solution the full step can overshoot back and forth

B) The tolerance is applied only to currents

C) LU factorization introduces the oscillation

D) Newton is globally convergent, so the matrix must be wrong
problems.a: Newton converges only locally; far from a solution the full step can overshoot back and forth
problems.e: Quadratic convergence holds only near a root. Far away, full Newton steps can cycle, which damping and limiting are designed to stop.

problems.q:
Newton starts a diode circuit at 0 V, and the first update proposes 8 V across the junction. What goes wrong if the simulator evaluates the diode there?

A) The exponential overflows or gives a huge current and conductance, and the next iterate is meaningless

B) The diode current becomes negative

C) The matrix becomes symmetric

D) Nothing; Newton always converges from any start
problems.a: The exponential overflows or gives a huge current and conductance, and the next iterate is meaningless
problems.e: At 8 V, $e^{V/V_T}$ is astronomically large. Junction limiting replaces such proposals with a logarithmically compressed voltage.

problems.q:
A latch has two stable states and a metastable one. Newton converges to the metastable point. Is the operating point wrong?

A) It is always a convergence failure

B) It is a valid DC solution; the equations have several, and Newton found the one nearest its path

C) DC analysis cannot have more than one solution

D) It means gmin is too large
problems.a: It is a valid DC solution; the equations have several, and Newton found the one nearest its path
problems.e: Nonlinear circuits with positive feedback have multiple DC solutions. Which one Newton finds depends on the initial guess, which is why .nodeset exists.

problems.q:
A large mixed circuit fails the operating point with a plain Newton solve from zero. Which aid adds a shunt conductance at every node and removes it gradually?

A) Gmin stepping

B) Timestep control

C) Junction limiting

D) Source stepping
problems.a: Gmin stepping
problems.e: Gmin stepping starts with a large conductance to ground at every node, which makes the problem nearly linear and well conditioned, then shrinks it in a continuation.

problems.q:
A large mixed circuit fails the operating point with a plain Newton solve from zero. Which aid adds a shunt conductance at every node and removes it gradually?

A) Timestep control

B) Gmin stepping

C) Source stepping

D) Junction limiting
problems.a: Gmin stepping
problems.e: Gmin stepping starts with a large conductance to ground at every node, which makes the problem nearly linear and well conditioned, then shrinks it in a continuation.

problems.q:
Both gmin and source stepping fail on a circuit with strong positive feedback. Which method treats the operating point as the end of a fictitious transient?

A) Increasing itl1 only

B) Pseudo-transient continuation

C) AC analysis

D) Junction limiting
problems.a: Pseudo-transient continuation
problems.e: Pseudo-transient adds artificial capacitance (or inductance) and integrates in time until the circuit settles. Time-stepping follows a physical path that rarely gets stuck.

problems.q:
Damping by clipping every node update to 0.1 V fixes divergence but a 50-node solve now takes 200 iterations. What has been traded?

A) Accuracy for robustness: the answer is now less accurate

B) Memory for speed

C) Nothing, since iteration count does not matter

D) Robustness for speed: small fixed steps lose Newton's quadratic convergence far from the root
problems.a: Robustness for speed: small fixed steps lose Newton's quadratic convergence far from the root
problems.e: Clipped steps creep toward the solution linearly. The converged answer is as accurate as before, but reaching it costs many more factorizations.

problems.q:
Gmin stepping converged, but the final solve with gmin at its default value did not. What does the earlier converged point mean?

A) It means reltol was too tight

B) It proves the circuit has no solution

C) Nothing for the real circuit: it solved a modified circuit with extra conductances

D) It is the answer to report
problems.a: Nothing for the real circuit: it solved a modified circuit with extra conductances
problems.e: Intermediate continuation solutions belong to a different circuit. Only a converged solve with the final, negligible gmin is the operating point.

problems.q:
Gmin stepping converged, but the final solve with gmin at its default value did not. What does the earlier converged point mean?

A) It proves the circuit has no solution

B) Nothing for the real circuit: it solved a modified circuit with extra conductances

C) It means reltol was too tight

D) It is the answer to report
problems.a: Nothing for the real circuit: it solved a modified circuit with extra conductances
problems.e: Intermediate continuation solutions belong to a different circuit. Only a converged solve with the final, negligible gmin is the operating point.

label: Running decks in ngspice and Xyce
lesson:
# Running decks in ngspice and Xyce

ngspice and Xyce are the two open-source simulators a tool designer is most likely to read, run and extend. ngspice descends from Berkeley SPICE3 with many extensions; Xyce was written at Sandia National Laboratories for large parallel simulations. Both read SPICE decks, both expose their numerical machinery through analysis cards and options, and both write raw files that scripts can parse. Knowing which knob reaches which part of the engine is how you debug a run instead of guessing.

## Analysis cards and what they compute

Each dot card requests an analysis. .op solves the DC operating point by Newton. .dc sweeps a source, re-solving the operating point at each value from the previous solution. .ac linearizes all devices at the operating point and solves the complex system $(G + j\omega C)x = b$ over a frequency sweep. .noise is a small-signal sweep that sums device noise densities to an output and refers them to an input. .tran tstep tstop integrates in time; tstep is the print and initial suggested step, not a fixed step, because the internal step is chosen by truncation-error control. A card .tran 1p 2n therefore asks for output every picosecond up to 2 ns, while the engine may take far fewer or more internal steps.

## Options that steer the numerical engine

The .options card reaches the solver directly. reltol (default $10^{-3}$), abstol (default 1 pA) and vntol (default 1 uV) set the Newton convergence tests and, through reltol, the truncation-error tolerance used in step control; trtol scales how strictly truncation error is enforced. gmin is the minimum conductance added across junctions and used by gmin stepping. itl1 and itl4 limit Newton iterations for the operating point and for each transient step. method=gear switches integration from trapezoidal to backward differentiation formulas, with maxord setting the order. Loosening reltol to $10^{-2}$ trades accuracy for speed everywhere; setting abstol to 1 uA on a nanoampere circuit silently accepts errors larger than the signal.

## Reading output and choosing a simulator

In batch mode, ngspice -b deck.cir -r out.raw runs without a user interface and writes every vector (time, node voltages, branch currents) to a raw file that post-processing reads. .measure statements compute scalar results inside the run, such as the delay between 50% crossings of two waveforms, so a characterization script needs only the log. When two simulators disagree, compare their default options and convergence strategies first: different gmin, tolerances and homotopy choices change results more often than bugs do. Xyce was designed for parallel execution with distributed-memory linear solvers, which matters for very large post-layout decks, and it offers homotopy methods for hard operating points.

## Going deeper

The ngspice manual; the Xyce Users' Guide and Reference Guide (Sandia National Laboratories).

problems.q:
A deck has .noise v(out) V1 dec 10 1k 1g. What does it report?

A) Monte Carlo statistics of v(out)

B) Output noise spectral density at v(out) and the equivalent input noise referred to source V1

C) The transient waveform of random noise

D) The DC operating point with noise sources removed
problems.a: Output noise spectral density at v(out) and the equivalent input noise referred to source V1
problems.e: Noise analysis is a small-signal frequency sweep that sums each device's noise power through its transfer function to the output, and refers it to the named input.

problems.q:
A deck has .noise v(out) V1 dec 10 1k 1g. What does it report?

A) Monte Carlo statistics of v(out)

B) Output noise spectral density at v(out) and the equivalent input noise referred to source V1

C) The DC operating point with noise sources removed

D) The transient waveform of random noise
problems.a: Output noise spectral density at v(out) and the equivalent input noise referred to source V1
problems.e: Noise analysis is a small-signal frequency sweep that sums each device's noise power through its transfer function to the output, and refers it to the named input.

problems.q:
Which analysis card makes the simulator linearize the circuit at its operating point and sweep frequency?

A) .dc

B) .op

C) .ac

D) .tran
problems.a: .ac
problems.e: .ac computes the DC operating point, linearizes every device there and solves the complex system at each frequency.

problems.q:
A deck fails the DC operating point with too many iterations. Which pair of options relates to that failure rather than to transient accuracy?

A) tstep and tstop

B) method and maxord

C) itl1 (the DC iteration limit) and gmin (the minimum shunt conductance)

D) trtol and chgtol
problems.a: itl1 (the DC iteration limit) and gmin (the minimum shunt conductance)
problems.e: itl1 bounds Newton iterations for the operating point and gmin sets the conductance used by gmin stepping. trtol and chgtol govern transient step control.

problems.q:
An LC oscillator deck shows trapezoidal ringing on a sharp edge. Which ngspice option addresses the integration method directly?

A) .options gmin=1e-15

B) .options method=gear

C) .options itl1=500

D) .options vntol=1e-9
problems.a: .options method=gear
problems.e: method=gear switches from trapezoidal to backward differentiation formulas, which damp the spurious oscillation trapezoidal produces on stiff components.

problems.q:
An LC oscillator deck shows trapezoidal ringing on a sharp edge. Which ngspice option addresses the integration method directly?

A) .options vntol=1e-9

B) .options method=gear

C) .options gmin=1e-15

D) .options itl1=500
problems.a: .options method=gear
problems.e: method=gear switches from trapezoidal to backward differentiation formulas, which damp the spurious oscillation trapezoidal produces on stiff components.

problems.q:
A team must simulate a very large post-layout analog block on a cluster with distributed memory. Which property of Xyce matters most?

A) It skips the DC operating point

B) It was designed for parallel execution, with distributed-memory solvers

C) It is the only simulator that reads SPICE decks

D) It uses fixed timesteps, which parallelize trivially
problems.a: It was designed for parallel execution, with distributed-memory solvers
problems.e: Xyce was written at Sandia National Laboratories as a parallel circuit simulator, so it partitions the problem and uses distributed linear solvers.

problems.q:
A characterization flow needs the 50% propagation delay of each run as one number. Which deck feature computes it inside the simulator?

A) A .print of every time point

B) A tighter reltol

C) A .measure statement with trig and targ conditions on the two waveforms

D) An extra .op analysis
problems.a: A .measure statement with trig and targ conditions on the two waveforms
problems.e: .measure evaluates expressions on the waveforms after the run, such as the time between a 50% crossing of the input and of the output, and logs the value.

problems.q:
A script runs ngspice in batch mode and needs every node voltage of a transient for later analysis. What should it ask for?

A) Only the final time point from the log

B) A raw output file, for example with ngspice -b deck.cir -r out.raw

C) A screenshot of the plot window

D) The .model cards printed to the log
problems.a: A raw output file, for example with ngspice -b deck.cir -r out.raw
problems.e: The raw file stores all vectors (node voltages, branch currents, time) in a documented format that post-processing tools read directly.

label: Voltage-controlled current source stamps
lesson:
# Voltage-controlled current source stamps

Controlled sources are how small-signal device models enter MNA: a transistor's transconductance is a voltage-controlled current source. The VCCS stamp is a four-entry pattern that couples the output nodes' rows to the controlling nodes' columns. It needs no new unknown, but it breaks the symmetry that resistors alone produce, which is one reason SPICE uses a general LU factorization.

## Four entries off the controlling nodes

The card G1 n+ n- nc+ nc- gm drives a current $g_m(v_{nc+} - v_{nc-})$ from n+ through the source to n-. That current leaves node n+, so in the KCL row of n+ it appears with a plus sign: $+g_m$ at column nc+ and $-g_m$ at column nc-. It enters node n-, so row n- gets $-g_m$ at nc+ and $+g_m$ at nc-. Any row or column belonging to ground is dropped. For G1 1 3 2 0 3m, the stamp is $+3$ mS at (1,2) and -3 mS at (3,2); the nc- column is ground and vanishes. A VCCS adds no unknown because its current is already expressed in node voltages.

## Adding a VCCS to a resistive matrix

Stamps accumulate, so an entry of the full matrix is the resistor contribution plus any controlled-source contribution at that position. If a 1 k$\Omega$ resistor joins nodes 2 and 3 and a VCCS G1 3 2 1 2 4.5m is present, entry (3,2) gets -1 from the resistor and -4.5 from the VCCS (row n+ = 3, column nc- = 2), so -5.5 mS, while (3,1) gets only $+4.5$ mS. When a VCCS output node coincides with one of its controlling nodes, the stamp lands on a diagonal and behaves like a conductance, positive or negative. A negative effective conductance is the signature of gain and positive feedback.

## Controlled sources break symmetry

Resistor stamps are symmetric, so a passive resistive network has $G = G^T$, and its matrix is positive definite once grounded. A VCCS puts entries in output rows and control columns without the mirror image, so $G_{ab} - G_{ba}$ equals the controlled-source contribution alone. For G1 4 3 2 1 3m, $G_{42} = +3$ mS but $G_{24}$ has no VCCS entry, so $G_{24} - G_{42} = -3$ mS. The loss of symmetry rules out Cholesky factorization and means the adjoint system uses $G^T$, not $G$. SPICE-class simulators therefore use sparse LU with pivoting chosen for both stability and sparsity.

## Going deeper

Vlach and Singhal, "Computer Methods for Circuit Analysis and Design" (2nd ed., 1994), chapter on MNA; Najm, "Circuit Simulation" (Wiley, 2010).

problems.q: A VCCS card G1 n+ n- nc+ nc- gm drives a current $g_m (v_{nc+} - v_{nc-})$ from n+ through the source into n-. A circuit with nodes 1 to 3 contains G1 1 0 3 0 0.5m (gm in mS, 0 is ground). Which entries does this card alone stamp into the nodal matrix entry $G_{13}$, in mS? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: The VCCS stamps $+g_m$ at (n+, nc+), $-g_m$ at (n+, nc-), $-g_m$ at (n-, nc+) and $+g_m$ at (n-, nc-), dropping any ground row or column. Entry (1, 3) is 0.5 mS.

problems.q: A VCCS card G1 n+ n- nc+ nc- gm drives a current $g_m (v_{nc+} - v_{nc-})$ from n+ through the source into n-. A circuit with nodes 1 to 4 contains G1 2 0 1 3 3.5m (gm in mS, 0 is ground). Which entries does this card alone stamp into the nodal matrix entry $G_{23}$, in mS? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: The VCCS stamps $+g_m$ at (n+, nc+), $-g_m$ at (n+, nc-), $-g_m$ at (n-, nc+) and $+g_m$ at (n-, nc-), dropping any ground row or column. Entry (2, 3) is -3.5 mS.

problems.q: A VCCS card G1 n+ n- nc+ nc- gm drives a current $g_m (v_{nc+} - v_{nc-})$ from n+ through the source into n-. A circuit with nodes 1 to 4 contains G1 1 2 4 3 4m (gm in mS, 0 is ground). Which entries does this card alone stamp into the nodal matrix entry $G_{23}$, in mS? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: The VCCS stamps $+g_m$ at (n+, nc+), $-g_m$ at (n+, nc-), $-g_m$ at (n-, nc+) and $+g_m$ at (n-, nc-), dropping any ground row or column. Entry (2, 3) is 4 mS.

problems.q: A VCCS card G1 n+ n- nc+ nc- gm drives a current $g_m (v_{nc+} - v_{nc-})$ from n+ through the source into n-. A circuit with nodes 1 to 3 has R1 between nodes 1 and 2, 0.5 k$\Omega$; R2 between nodes 2 and 3, 2.5 k$\Omega$; R3 from node 2 to ground, 1 k$\Omega$; R4 between nodes 3 and 2, 0.5 k$\Omega$, and also G1 2 0 1 0 1.5m (gm in mS). What is the nodal matrix entry $G_{23}$ in mS? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: Stamp the resistors, then add the VCCS entries on top. Entry (2, 3) is -2.4 mS.

problems.q: A VCCS card G1 n+ n- nc+ nc- gm drives a current $g_m (v_{nc+} - v_{nc-})$ from n+ through the source into n-. A circuit with nodes 1 to 4 has R1 between nodes 1 and 2, 0.25 k$\Omega$; R2 between nodes 1 and 3, 5 k$\Omega$; R3 between nodes 1 and 4, 0.5 k$\Omega$; R4 from node 1 to ground, 1 k$\Omega$; R5 between nodes 1 and 2, 2 k$\Omega$, and also G1 4 0 2 0 3m (gm in mS). What is the nodal matrix entry $G_{42}$ in mS? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: Stamp the resistors, then add the VCCS entries on top. Entry (4, 2) is 3 mS.

problems.q: A VCCS card G1 n+ n- nc+ nc- gm drives a current $g_m (v_{nc+} - v_{nc-})$ from n+ through the source into n-. A circuit with nodes 1 to 3 has R1 between nodes 1 and 2, 4 k$\Omega$; R2 between nodes 2 and 3, 1 k$\Omega$; R3 from node 1 to ground, 0.25 k$\Omega$; R4 between nodes 3 and 2, 2 k$\Omega$, and also G1 2 1 3 0 1.5m (gm in mS). What is the nodal matrix entry $G_{13}$ in mS? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: Stamp the resistors, then add the VCCS entries on top. Entry (1, 3) is -1.5 mS.

problems.q: A VCCS card G1 n+ n- nc+ nc- gm drives a current $g_m (v_{nc+} - v_{nc-})$ from n+ through the source into n-. A circuit with nodes 1 to 3 has R1 between nodes 1 and 2, 2 k$\Omega$; R2 between nodes 1 and 3, 0.25 k$\Omega$; R3 from node 2 to ground, 0.25 k$\Omega$; R4 between nodes 1 and 3, 1 k$\Omega$, and also G1 1 3 2 3 0.5m (gm in mS). Resistors alone give a symmetric matrix. What is $G_{21} - G_{12}$ in mS? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: Resistor stamps cancel in the difference, so only the VCCS remains: -0.5 mS. Controlled sources make the MNA matrix unsymmetric, which is why SPICE uses a general sparse LU rather than Cholesky.

problems.q: A VCCS card G1 n+ n- nc+ nc- gm drives a current $g_m (v_{nc+} - v_{nc-})$ from n+ through the source into n-. A circuit with nodes 1 to 4 has R1 between nodes 1 and 2, 1 k$\Omega$; R2 between nodes 2 and 3, 2.5 k$\Omega$; R3 between nodes 2 and 4, 2.5 k$\Omega$; R4 from node 2 to ground, 2 k$\Omega$; R5 from node 4 to ground, 2.5 k$\Omega$, and also G1 2 4 1 4 3.5m (gm in mS). Resistors alone give a symmetric matrix. What is $G_{21} - G_{12}$ in mS? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: Resistor stamps cancel in the difference, so only the VCCS remains: 3.5 mS. Controlled sources make the MNA matrix unsymmetric, which is why SPICE uses a general sparse LU rather than Cholesky.

problems.q: A VCCS card G1 n+ n- nc+ nc- gm drives a current $g_m (v_{nc+} - v_{nc-})$ from n+ through the source into n-. A circuit with nodes 1 to 4 has R1 between nodes 1 and 2, 0.5 k$\Omega$; R2 between nodes 2 and 3, 10 k$\Omega$; R3 between nodes 1 and 4, 2 k$\Omega$; R4 from node 2 to ground, 1 k$\Omega$; R5 between nodes 3 and 1, 2.5 k$\Omega$, and also G1 1 0 2 4 1m (gm in mS). Resistors alone give a symmetric matrix. What is $G_{21} - G_{12}$ in mS? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: Resistor stamps cancel in the difference, so only the VCCS remains: -1 mS. Controlled sources make the MNA matrix unsymmetric, which is why SPICE uses a general sparse LU rather than Cholesky.

label: VCVS stamps and controlled branch rows
lesson:
# VCVS stamps and controlled branch rows

A voltage-controlled voltage source forces an output voltage proportional to a controlling voltage. Like an independent voltage source it needs a branch-current unknown, and like a VCCS it couples to controlling nodes. Its stamp combines both patterns, and it is the building block of ideal amplifiers, behavioral macromodels and many textbook test circuits. Reading its entries and its branch current is a direct test of the MNA conventions.

## The VCVS branch row

The card E1 n+ n- nc+ nc- mu imposes $v_{n+} - v_{n-} - \mu(v_{nc+} - v_{nc-}) = 0$. MNA adds its branch current as an unknown and this constraint as a row. The row has $+1$ at column n+, -1 at n-, $-\mu$ at nc+ and $+\mu$ at nc-, with a zero right-hand side. The branch column, as for any voltage source, has $+1$ in row n+ and -1 in row n-. Ground entries are dropped. With three nodes and the cards V1 2 0 1 then E1 1 0 2 0 2, unknowns are $v_1, v_2, v_3$, then the V1 and E1 currents; the E1 row (row 5) has $+1$ at column 1 and -2 at column 2.

## Counting unknowns with controlled sources

The unknown count follows one rule: anything that forces a voltage needs its current. Node voltages count first; then add one branch current for each independent voltage source, each VCVS and each inductor (SPICE keeps inductor currents as unknowns). VCCS, current sources, resistors and capacitors add none. A circuit with 5 nodes, 2 voltage sources, 1 VCVS, 2 inductors, any number of resistors, capacitors and current sources, and a VCCS has $5 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 10$ unknowns. Current-controlled sources add a further branch only for the CCVS, which forces a voltage; the CCCS reuses the controlling source's current.

## Solving an ideal amplifier stage

Consider V1 1 0 Vin, E1 2 0 1 0 mu and a load from node 2 to ground. The E1 row forces $v_2 = \mu v_1 = \mu V_{in}$ at once, and the load current is $v_2/R_L$. E1 delivers that current out of its + terminal, so with SPICE's convention (positive current flows into the + terminal) its branch current is $-\mu V_{in}/R_L$. With $V_{in} = 0.5$ V, $\mu = 2$ and a load of 0.5 k$\Omega$ plus 2.5 k$\Omega$ in series, $v_2 = 1$ V, the source delivers $1/3$ mA and reports -0.333 mA. An ideal VCVS has zero output resistance, so the load never changes $v_2$; real op-amp macromodels add an output resistance.

label: Sparsity and structure of the MNA matrix
lesson:
# Sparsity and structure of the MNA matrix

Circuit matrices are extremely sparse: a node connects to a handful of neighbours, so a row of a million-node matrix holds perhaps five nonzeros. The pattern of nonzeros is fixed by the netlist before any value is known, and simulators analyze it once, choose an elimination order, and reuse the symbolic factorization for every Newton iteration and time step. Counting nonzeros and spotting zero diagonals is how a tool designer reasons about memory, fill-in and pivoting.

## Counting structural nonzeros

A structural nonzero is a position that some stamp touches, whatever its value. In the nodal conductance matrix every node has a nonzero diagonal, and each distinct pair of non-ground nodes joined by at least one resistor adds two symmetric off-diagonal positions. Resistors to ground touch only diagonals, and parallel resistors share positions. So the count is $n + 2p$, where $p$ is the number of distinct connected node pairs. A three-node chain 1-2-3 with a resistor to ground has $3 + 2 \cdot 2 = 7$ nonzeros out of 9. Simulators store only these entries, in compressed column or row form, with the pattern computed once from the netlist.

## Nonzeros of the augmented matrix

Voltage sources add a branch row and column. A source from node $a$ to ground adds $+1$ at $(a, k)$ and $(k, a)$, where $k$ is its branch index: 2 nonzeros. A source between two non-ground nodes adds 4. Its own diagonal $(k, k)$ stays empty. A five-node network with 13 nonzeros in its node block plus one grounded voltage source has $13 + 2 = 15$ nonzeros in a 6 by 6 matrix. Because stamps never change position between iterations, the simulator can map every element to the matrix addresses it writes during setup, so the load phase is a sequence of direct indexed additions.

## Zero diagonals and pivoting

Every branch row that expresses a voltage constraint (independent voltage source, VCVS, or inductor at DC) has no term in its own current, so its diagonal is a structural zero. The count of zero diagonals is the number of such branches. Node rows have positive diagonals from conductances and, in practice, from the gmin added across junctions. Zero diagonals mean the matrix cannot be factored in an arbitrary order without pivoting. SPICE-class solvers choose a pivot order that balances numerical stability against fill-in, the new nonzeros created by elimination, often by ordering for sparsity and then checking pivot magnitudes. A bad order can turn a sparse matrix dense.

## Going deeper

Davis, "Direct Methods for Sparse Linear Systems" (SIAM, 2006); Davis and Palamadai Natarajan, "Algorithm 907: KLU, a direct sparse solver for circuit simulation problems" (ACM TOMS, 2010).

label: Newton convergence tests
lesson:
# Newton convergence tests

Newton never reaches the exact solution; a simulator must decide when to stop. SPICE's convergence tests combine relative and absolute tolerances on both node voltages and device currents, and their defaults are worth memorizing because they set the accuracy of every result. Understanding how quickly Newton converges near the solution also tells you how many iterations a healthy operating point should take.

## The voltage tolerance band

SPICE accepts a node voltage when successive iterates agree within a band:
$$|v_k - v_{k-1}| \le \text{RELTOL} \cdot \max(|v_k|, |v_{k-1}|) + \text{VNTOL},$$
with defaults RELTOL $= 10^{-3}$ and VNTOL $= 1$ uV. The relative term dominates for ordinary voltages; VNTOL keeps the test meaningful near 0 V, where a pure relative test could never pass. For iterates 1.2000 V and 1.1995 V, the band is $1.2 \times 10^{-3} + 10^{-6}$ V, about 1201 uV, and the change of 500 uV passes. Every node must pass, and the test is applied on consecutive iterates, so at least two iterations are always needed.

## Quadratic convergence in iterations

Near a simple root with a smooth Jacobian, Newton converges quadratically: $e_{k+1} \approx C e_k^2$, where $e_k$ is the error and $C$ depends on the curvature. Each iteration roughly doubles the number of correct digits. With $C = 2$ per volt and $e_0 = 0.1$ V, the errors are 0.02, $8 \times 10^{-4}$, $1.3 \times 10^{-6}$, $3.3 \times 10^{-12}$: four iterations reach picovolts. This is why a converging operating point typically finishes in a few iterations once it is close, and why a run that needs hundreds of iterations signals a problem: the iterate is far from the root, being damped or limited, or the Jacobian is wrong.

## The current tolerance

SPICE also checks device currents, because a voltage can settle while a steep exponential current is still far off. The test is $|i_k - i_{k-1}| \le \text{RELTOL} \cdot \max(|i_k|, |i_{k-1}|) + \text{ABSTOL}$, with ABSTOL $= 1$ pA by default. For a branch current near 0.124 mA, the band is $0.124 \times 10^{-3}$ mA plus 1 pA, about 124 nA. ABSTOL matters for circuits biased at tiny currents: a leakage-dominated node carrying 10 pA has a band of about 1 pA, dominated by ABSTOL. Raising ABSTOL to speed convergence on a low-current circuit quietly accepts currents that are wrong by more than their own size.

## Going deeper

The ngspice manual, the section on convergence options; Najm, "Circuit Simulation" (Wiley, 2010), chapter 4.

label: Linearizing a MOSFET at a Newton iterate
lesson:
# Linearizing a MOSFET at a Newton iterate

A MOSFET is a three-port nonlinearity: its drain current depends on both gate-source and drain-source voltages. Linearizing it for Newton produces a transconductance, an output conductance and an equivalent current, the same companion idea as for the diode with one more partial derivative. Device models in SPICE return exactly these derivatives, and their accuracy decides how fast Newton converges.

## Transconductance from the square law

In saturation the square law with channel-length modulation is $I_D = \tfrac{k}{2}(V_{GS} - V_T)^2(1 + \lambda V_{DS})$. The transconductance is the partial derivative with respect to the gate-source voltage at the iterate:
$$g_m = \frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{GS}} = k(V_{GS} - V_T)(1 + \lambda V_{DS}).$$
For $k = 1$ mA/V$^2$, $V_T = 0.5$ V, $V_{GS} = 0.9$ V, $V_{DS} = 1$ V and $\lambda = 0.1$ 1/V, the overdrive is 0.4 V and $g_m = 1 \times 0.4 \times 1.1 = 0.44$ mS. It stamps like a VCCS controlled by $v_{GS}$ from drain to source.

## Output conductance

The partial derivative with respect to the drain-source voltage is
$$g_{ds} = \frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{DS}} = \tfrac{k}{2}(V_{GS} - V_T)^2 \lambda.$$
In the example, $g_{ds} = 0.5 \times 0.16 \times 0.1 = 0.008$ mS, or 8 uS, an output resistance of 125 k$\Omega$. It stamps like a resistor between drain and source. Real compact models compute $g_{ds}$ from far more physics, but they must keep it continuous across the boundary between triode and saturation: a jump in $g_{ds}$ there makes Newton hop back and forth between regions, a classic convergence failure in older models.

## The MOSFET equivalent current

The linearized drain current is $I_D \approx g_m V_{GS} + g_{ds} V_{DS} + I_{eq}$, where
$$I_{eq} = I_D(V_k) - g_m V_{GS} - g_{ds} V_{DS}$$
is the intercept of the tangent plane. In the example $I_D = 0.5 \times 0.16 \times 1.1 = 0.088$ mA, so $I_{eq} = 0.088 - 0.44 \times 0.9 - 0.008 \times 1 = -0.316$ mA. The full stamp is the VCCS $g_m$, the conductance $g_{ds}$ and a current source $I_{eq}$ from drain to source. Simulators also stamp gate and bulk derivatives and charge derivatives for transient. A model with a wrong derivative still converges to the right answer, because the residual uses the true current, but it converges slowly.

## Going deeper

Najm, "Circuit Simulation" (Wiley, 2010), chapter 4; Tsividis and McAndrew, "Operation and Modeling of the MOS Transistor" (3rd ed., Oxford, 2011).

label: Inductor companion models
lesson:
# Inductor companion models

Inductors get companion models too, by discretizing $v = L\, di/dt$ instead of $i = C\, dv/dt$. The result is again a conductance with a history source, now expressing the new inductor current in terms of the new voltage. Simulators that keep inductor currents as branch unknowns stamp the equivalent branch equation instead, but the coefficients are the same, and computing them by hand fixes the duality between the two reactive elements.

## Backward Euler inductor

Backward Euler applied to $di/dt = v/L$ gives $i_{n+1} = i_n + (h/L) v_{n+1}$. Read as a companion, the inductor is a conductance $G_{eq} = h/L$ in parallel with a current source $I_{eq} = i_n$ that carries the previous current, with $i_{n+1} = G_{eq} v_{n+1} + I_{eq}$. Units: nanoseconds over microhenries is millisiemens. A 1 uH inductor at $h = 0.5$ ns has $G_{eq} = 0.5$ mS. If it carries 2 mA and the step solve finds 0.4 V across it, the new current is $2 + 0.5 \times 0.4 = 2.2$ mA. Small steps make $G_{eq}$ small: over a short step an inductor holds its current, as a capacitor holds its voltage.

## Trapezoidal inductor conductance

The trapezoidal rule averages the voltage over the step: $i_{n+1} = i_n + \tfrac{h}{2L}(v_n + v_{n+1})$. The coefficient of $v_{n+1}$ is the companion conductance,
$$G_{eq} = \frac{h}{2L},$$
half the backward Euler value for the same step. A 5 uH inductor at $h = 0.2$ ns gives $G_{eq} = 0.02$ mS. In an MNA implementation that keeps the inductor current $i$ as an unknown, the branch row becomes $v_+ - v_- - \tfrac{2L}{h} i_{n+1} = -\tfrac{2L}{h} i_n - v_n$, which carries the same information: the diagonal of the branch row is now $-2L/h$ instead of the zero it has at DC.

## The trapezoidal history current

The remaining terms of the trapezoidal update form the history source:
$$I_{eq} = i_n + \frac{h}{2L} v_n.$$
It needs both the previous current and the previous voltage. For 0.2 uH at $h = 0.2$ ns, with 2.5 mA and 1.9 V at $t_n$: $G_{eq} = 0.5$ mS and $I_{eq} = 2.5 + 0.5 \times 1.9 = 3.45$ mA. As with the capacitor, the trapezoidal history carries the previous step's derivative information, so a sudden voltage step across an inductor makes the computed current oscillate from step to step instead of settling. Backward Euler's history, the current alone, has no such memory, which is why it damps such transients.

## Going deeper

Najm, "Circuit Simulation" (Wiley, 2010), chapter 5; Vlach and Singhal, "Computer Methods for Circuit Analysis and Design" (2nd ed., 1994).

label: Trapezoidal ringing
lesson:
# Trapezoidal ringing

The trapezoidal rule is A-stable, yet on stiff circuits it produces a sawtooth that alternates in sign from step to step. The cause is its amplification factor, which tends to -1 for very fast modes instead of to 0. Recognizing this ringing, and knowing why simulators switch to backward Euler at breakpoints or offer Gear methods, is part of reading transient waveforms critically.

## The trapezoidal amplification factor

For the test mode $x' = -x/\tau$, a trapezoidal step multiplies the solution by
$$R = \frac{1 - h/2\tau}{1 + h/2\tau}.$$
For $h \ll \tau$ this is close to $e^{-h/\tau}$. For $h = 2\tau$ it is exactly 0. For $h > 2\tau$ it is negative, so the computed value flips sign every step, and as $h/\tau \to \infty$ it approaches -1: the fast mode barely decays. With $\tau = 0.1$ ns and $h = 0.15$ ns, $R = 0.25/1.75 = 0.143$; with $h = 1$ ns, $R = -4/6 = -0.667$. The method stays stable, $|R| < 1$, but a fast parasitic mode that should vanish in one step lingers as an oscillation.

## Ringing over several steps

After $k$ steps the fast mode is multiplied by $R^k$. With $h/\tau = 4$, $R = -1/3$: starting from 2 V, the computed values are -0.667, 0.222, -0.074, 0.025 V, while the true value is $2e^{-16}$, effectively zero, after four steps. With $h/\tau = 40$, $R = -0.905$, and the sawtooth survives dozens of steps. On a waveform plot this appears as a zigzag on a node that should be smooth, often right after a sharp edge, on nodes with tiny parasitic capacitances or stiff inductive loops. Shrinking the step removes it, but at the cost the large step was meant to avoid.

## Damping with a backward Euler step

Backward Euler's factor $1/(1 + h/\tau)$ tends to 0 for fast modes: it is L-stable and kills stiff components in one step. SPICE-class simulators exploit this by taking a backward-Euler step right after a breakpoint, where a discontinuity has just excited the fast modes, then returning to trapezoidal. With $h/\tau = 1.5$, one backward-Euler step multiplies by 0.4 and each trapezoidal step by $0.25/1.75 = 0.143$: starting from 2.5 V, one of each gives 0.143 V. The alternative is to use a Gear method throughout, damping ringing everywhere but adding numerical damping to genuine oscillations, such as those of a high-Q resonator.

## Going deeper

Hairer and Wanner, "Solving Ordinary Differential Equations II" (Springer, 1996), on A- and L-stability; Najm, "Circuit Simulation" (Wiley, 2010), chapter 5.

label: BDF and Gear integration
lesson:
# BDF and Gear integration

Backward differentiation formulas (BDF), introduced to circuit simulation by Gear, approximate the derivative at the new time point from several past points. They are the standard alternative to trapezoidal in SPICE (method=gear) because they damp stiff modes, at the cost of needing more history and, above second order, losing A-stability. The second-order formula, BDF2, has a companion model as simple as backward Euler's.

## The BDF2 derivative formula

BDF2 differentiates the quadratic through $x_{n-1}$, $x_n$ and $x_{n+1}$. At constant step $h$,
$$x'_{n+1} \approx \frac{3x_{n+1} - 4x_n + x_{n-1}}{2h}.$$
Applied to a capacitor, $i_{n+1} = C x'_{n+1}$, so the coefficient of $v_{n+1}$ is the companion conductance $G_{eq} = 3C/(2h)$, one and a half times the backward-Euler value. For 5 pF at $h = 0.1$ ns, $G_{eq} = 75$ mS. BDF of order 1 is backward Euler; orders 1 and 2 are A-stable and L-stable, while orders 3 to 6 are only stable in a wedge of the left half plane, which is usually acceptable for circuits.

## The BDF2 history current

The remaining terms form the history: $i_{n+1} = G_{eq} v_{n+1} - I_{eq}$ with
$$I_{eq} = \frac{C}{2h}(4v_n - v_{n-1}).$$
For 4 pF at $h = 0.2$ ns with $v_n = 0.8$ V and $v_{n-1} = 0.95$ V, $C/(2h) = 10$ mS and $4v_n - v_{n-1} = 2.25$ V, so $I_{eq} = 22.5$ mA. The history needs two past voltages but no past current. Because it needs two points, BDF2 cannot start itself: simulators take a backward-Euler first step. With variable steps the coefficients change with the step ratio, and simulators store the past points and recompute them.

## One BDF2 step on an RC node

For a source $V_s$ through $R$ into $C$, KCL gives $(1/R + 3C/(2h)) v_{n+1} = V_s/R + I_{eq}$. With $V_s = 3.5$ V, $R = 0.5$ k$\Omega$, $C = 0.5$ pF, $h = 0.1$ ns, $v_n = 1.8$ V and $v_{n-1} = 1.65$ V: $1/R = 2$ mS, $G_{eq} = 7.5$ mS, $I_{eq} = 2.5 \times 5.55 = 13.875$ mA, so $v_{n+1} = (7 + 13.875)/9.5 = 2.197$ V. For fast modes BDF2's amplification factor tends to 0, so there is no ringing; for genuine oscillations it adds artificial damping, so a high-Q oscillator simulated with Gear can decay that would not decay with trapezoidal.

## Going deeper

Gear, "Numerical Initial Value Problems in Ordinary Differential Equations" (Prentice Hall, 1971); Brayton, Gustavson and Hachtel, "A new efficient algorithm for solving differential-algebraic systems using implicit backward differentiation formulas" (Proceedings of the IEEE, 1972).

label: Breakpoints and step restarts
lesson:
# Breakpoints and step restarts

Step control assumes smooth waveforms. Circuits are full of corners: PWL and PULSE sources, switching events, the start of the simulation. Simulators handle them with breakpoints, time points the step must land on exactly, and with special treatment right after them. Initial conditions are the other boundary of a transient run, and SPICE offers several ways to set them, each with different meaning.

## Breakpoints at source corners

A PWL corner or the start and end of a PULSE edge is a discontinuity in the derivative of a source. Stepping across it smears the corner and corrupts the divided-difference error estimates, which assume smoothness, so the step controller would waste rejections finding it. SPICE instead registers every source corner as a breakpoint and shortens any step that would cross one. A PULSE with a 1 ns period has four corners per period, so a 100 ns run carries about 400 breakpoints from that one source. Decks with many fast, unsynchronized sources pack breakpoints densely and force small steps everywhere, which is one motivation for event-driven fast SPICE.

## Restarting after a discontinuity

At a breakpoint the past history no longer describes the waveform, so simulators restart integration: they cut the step to a small value, reset the order of multistep methods, and often take a backward-Euler step, whose L-stability damps the fast modes the edge excites. Discontinuities that are not known in advance, such as a switch model changing state when its control crosses a threshold, are found by event location: detect the crossing in a step, interpolate or bisect to find its time, and place a breakpoint there. When Newton fails at a new time point, the step is rejected and retried smaller; when the step falls below the minimum, the run aborts with a timestep-too-small error.

## Initial conditions and UIC

By default, transient starts from the DC operating point, which is consistent with every algebraic constraint. With uic on the .tran card the operating point is skipped and integration starts from the given initial conditions, with unspecified values at zero; inconsistent conditions then produce a jump on the first step that can look like a real transient. Without uic, .ic values are held during the operating-point solve and released at $t = 0$. A .nodeset is weaker still: only an initial guess for the operating point. An oscillator started exactly at its unstable equilibrium never oscillates in a deterministic simulator, so designers kick it with an initial condition.

## Going deeper

The ngspice manual, sections on .tran, .ic and .nodeset; Najm, "Circuit Simulation" (Wiley, 2010), chapter 5.

problems.q:
A PULSE source has 10 ps rise and fall times and a 1 ns period over a 100 ns run. How many breakpoints does it contribute, roughly?

A) Two: start and end of the run

B) None: PULSE sources are smooth

C) About 400: four corners per period over 100 periods

D) About 100: one per period
problems.a: About 400: four corners per period over 100 periods
problems.e: Each period has the start and end of the rise and of the fall, four slope discontinuities, each registered as a breakpoint.

problems.q:
A digital-heavy deck has many fast PULSE sources with unrelated periods. What happens to the timestep?

A) It grows, because breakpoints relax tolerances

B) It is repeatedly cut to hit breakpoints, so the run takes many small steps even where signals are idle

C) Nothing; breakpoints only affect output

D) It becomes fixed at tstep
problems.a: It is repeatedly cut to hit breakpoints, so the run takes many small steps even where signals are idle
problems.e: Every source corner forces a step boundary. Many unsynchronized edges pack breakpoints densely, which is one reason fast SPICE uses event-driven methods.

problems.q:
Why does the step controller not simply detect a source corner from a large truncation error?

A) LTE is never computed near sources

B) Breakpoints are only used for printing

C) Corners have zero truncation error

D) The error estimate assumes smooth waveforms, so a step across a kink gives a misleading estimate and wasted rejections
problems.a: The error estimate assumes smooth waveforms, so a step across a kink gives a misleading estimate and wasted rejections
problems.e: Divided-difference estimates of higher derivatives are garbage across a discontinuity. Knowing the corner in advance is cheaper and more accurate.

problems.q:
A switch model changes its conductance abruptly when its control crosses a threshold. How can a simulator handle the crossing accurately?

A) Ignore it; the step controller always hits it exactly

B) Switch to AC analysis

C) Locate the crossing time, for example by interpolation or bisection, and place a breakpoint there

D) Use a fixed step equal to the run length
problems.a: Locate the crossing time, for example by interpolation or bisection, and place a breakpoint there
problems.e: Internal discontinuities are not known in advance. Event location turns them into breakpoints after the fact, at the cost of a rejected step.

problems.q:
A Newton solve at a new time point fails to converge. What does a typical simulator do next?

A) Accept the unconverged solution

B) Reject the step and retry from the last accepted point with a smaller step

C) Double the step to escape the difficulty

D) Restart from the DC operating point
problems.a: Reject the step and retry from the last accepted point with a smaller step
problems.e: A smaller step makes the previous solution a better initial guess and the companion conductances larger, which both help Newton converge.

problems.q:
A step is rejected three times in a row at the same time point, and the step falls below the minimum allowed. What does the user see?

A) A singular-matrix error at DC

B) A 'timestep too small' failure

C) A silently wrong waveform

D) A finished run with fewer output points
problems.a: A 'timestep too small' failure
problems.e: When Newton or the error test keeps failing, the controller keeps shrinking the step. Below the minimum step the simulator aborts with a timestep-too-small message.

problems.q:
What is the difference between .ic without uic and .nodeset?

A) .nodeset fixes the value for the whole transient

B) .ic is ignored unless the circuit is linear

C) They are identical

D) .ic holds the node at the value during the operating-point solve and releases it at t = 0; .nodeset is only an initial guess
problems.a: .ic holds the node at the value during the operating-point solve and releases it at t = 0; .nodeset is only an initial guess
problems.e: Without uic, .ic constrains the operating point to the requested values. .nodeset merely helps Newton start near a solution and imposes nothing.

problems.q:

A) .ic is ignored unless the circuit is linear

B) They are identical

C) .nodeset fixes the value for the whole transient

D) .ic holds the node at the value during the operating-point solve and releases it at t = 0; .nodeset is only an initial guess

problems.e: Without uic, .ic constrains the operating point to the requested values. .nodeset merely helps Newton start near a solution and imposes nothing.

problems.q:
An oscillator deck starts at its exact DC operating point and never oscillates in simulation. Why?

A) The timestep was too small

B) The trapezoidal rule cannot simulate oscillators

C) The equilibrium is a solution, and with no noise or kick nothing perturbs it

D) Breakpoints damp all oscillations
problems.a: The equilibrium is a solution, and with no noise or kick nothing perturbs it
problems.e: A deterministic simulator stays at an unstable equilibrium. Designers kick the circuit with an initial condition or a brief source pulse.

label: Small-signal models from the operating point
prereqs: Linearizing a MOSFET at a Newton iterate
lesson:
# Small-signal models from the operating point

AC analysis begins where the DC operating point ends. Every nonlinear device is replaced by its small-signal model, the derivatives of its currents and charges at the bias point, which are exactly the conductances Newton already computed in its last iteration. For a MOSFET those are the transconductance and output conductance. Getting them right by hand is how you check an AC result against intuition.

## Transconductance at the bias point

For a square-law device in saturation, $I_D = \tfrac{k}{2} V_{ov}^2$ with $V_{ov} = V_{GS} - V_T$, so $g_m = k V_{ov}$, which can be written without $k$ as
$$g_m = \frac{2 I_D}{V_{ov}}.$$
With $I_D = 0.5$ mA and $V_{ov} = 0.2$ V, $g_m = 5$ mS. The form matters: at fixed current, a smaller overdrive gives more transconductance, which is why low-power analog designs bias near threshold. The simulator does not use this formula; it takes $\partial I_D/\partial V_{GS}$ from the compact model at the converged operating point, which agrees with the square law only for long-channel devices in strong inversion.

## Output resistance

Channel-length modulation makes the drain current rise slowly with drain voltage, $I_D \propto (1 + \lambda V_{DS})$, so the output conductance is $g_{ds} \approx \lambda I_D$ and the small-signal output resistance is
$$r_o \approx \frac{1}{\lambda I_D}.$$
With $\lambda = 0.1$ 1/V and $I_D = 0.5$ mA, $r_o = 20$ k$\Omega$ (one over millisiemens is kilohms). In AC analysis $r_o$ stamps as a conductance between drain and source, $g_m$ as a VCCS controlled by the gate-source voltage, and the device capacitances, derived from the charge model, as $j\omega C$ entries. All are frozen at the operating point: AC analysis is linear by construction.

## Intrinsic gain

The product $g_m r_o$ is the largest voltage gain a single transistor can give, its intrinsic gain. With the square-law forms, $g_m r_o = \tfrac{2 I_D}{V_{ov}} \cdot \tfrac{1}{\lambda I_D} = \tfrac{2}{\lambda V_{ov}}$: the current cancels. For $\lambda = 0.1$ 1/V and $V_{ov} = 0.2$ V, $g_m r_o = 100$, or 40 dB. Shorter channels have larger $\lambda$ and lower intrinsic gain. A designer reading AC output should expect a common-source stage's DC gain to stay below $g_m r_o$; a simulated gain far above it usually means a mistaken bias point, such as a device in the wrong region, rather than a good design.

## Going deeper

Razavi, "Design of Analog CMOS Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., McGraw-Hill, 2017), chapters 2 and 3; Najm, "Circuit Simulation" (Wiley, 2010), chapter on AC analysis.

label: The complex MNA system
lesson:
# The complex MNA system

AC analysis solves the linearized circuit at each frequency in a sweep. In the phasor domain a capacitor's current is $j\omega C$ times its voltage, so MNA becomes a complex linear system $(G + j\omega C)x = b$, with $G$ and $C$ the same matrices transient analysis uses. One complex sparse factorization per frequency point is the entire cost of an AC sweep, which is why AC is so much cheaper than transient.

## Admittance entries

A capacitor stamps like a resistor whose conductance is the admittance $j\omega C$: $+j\omega C$ on its two diagonals and $-j\omega C$ off the diagonal. So the diagonal entry of a node with a resistor and a capacitor to ground is $Y_{11} = G + j\omega C$. Units pair conveniently: $2\pi$ times megahertz times picofarads is microsiemens. A 1 pF capacitor at 10 MHz contributes $\omega C = 2\pi \times 10^{7} \times 10^{-12} = 62.8$ uS to the imaginary part, while a 2 k$\Omega$ resistor contributes 500 uS to the real part. Inductors in branch rows contribute $-j\omega L$ on their diagonal, and controlled sources and conductances stay real.

## Solving one complex node

A current source $I$ into a node with $R$ and $C$ to ground gives $V = I/(G + j\omega C)$, so $|V| = I/\sqrt{G^2 + (\omega C)^2}$. With $I = 5$ uA, $R = 2$ k$\Omega$ ($G = 500$ uS) and $C = 5$ pF at 10 MHz ($\omega C = 314$ uS), $|Y| = 590.5$ uS and $|V| = 8.47$ mV. Microamperes over microsiemens give volts. A simulator performs the same division in complex arithmetic inside an LU factorization. Since AC analysis is linear, the source amplitude is arbitrary: SPICE users typically set it to 1 so that node voltages read directly as transfer functions.

## Phase of the response

The phase of $V = I/(G + j\omega C)$ is the source phase minus the phase of the admittance: $\angle V = -\arctan(\omega C/G)$. For $R = 2$ k$\Omega$, $C = 0.5$ pF at 100 MHz, $\omega C = 314$ uS against $G = 500$ uS, so the phase is -32.1 degrees. At the corner frequency $\omega = G/C$ the phase is -45 degrees and the magnitude is down by $\sqrt{2}$. AC output reports real and imaginary parts, from which magnitude in dB and phase in degrees are derived. Phase is where errors in device capacitances show up first, which is why AC results are a sensitive check of a model's charge equations.

## Going deeper

Najm, "Circuit Simulation" (Wiley, 2010), chapter on frequency-domain analysis; Vlach and Singhal, "Computer Methods for Circuit Analysis and Design" (2nd ed., 1994).

label: AC small-signal analysis
prereqs: Small-signal models from the operating point
Transfer functions and the Laplace domain
lesson:
# AC small-signal analysis

AC small-signal analysis combines the two previous ideas: linearize every device at the operating point, then solve the complex MNA system over frequency. Its output is the transfer function of the linearized circuit: gain, bandwidth, phase. A common-source stage with a load capacitor is the canonical example, and its gain and pole frequency are what a designer checks first in any AC plot.

## Low-frequency gain

For a common-source stage with transconductance $g_m$, drain resistor $R_D$ and transistor output resistance $r_o$, the output node sees $R_{out} = R_D \parallel r_o$ and the low-frequency gain is $A_0 = -g_m R_{out}$. With $g_m = 2$ mS, $R_D = 20$ k$\Omega$ and $r_o = 80$ k$\Omega$, $R_{out} = 16$ k$\Omega$ and $|A_0| = 32$, which is $20 \log_{10} 32 = 30.1$ dB. Millisiemens times kilohms is dimensionless. The minus sign is a phase of 180 degrees at low frequency. A simulator reports the same number at the low end of the sweep, provided the operating point placed the device in saturation.

## Gain at a frequency

A load capacitance $C_L$ at the output adds a pole: $A(j\omega) = -g_m R_{out}/(1 + j\omega R_{out} C_L)$. Its magnitude is
$$|A| = \frac{|A_0|}{\sqrt{1 + (f/f_p)^2}}, \qquad f_p = \frac{1}{2\pi R_{out} C_L}.$$
With $R_{out} = 16$ k$\Omega$ and $C_L = 1$ pF, $R_{out} C_L = 16$ ns and $f_p = 9.95$ MHz. At 20 MHz, $|A| = 32/\sqrt{1 + 4.04} = 14.3$. Far above the pole the gain falls by a factor of 10 per decade, and the product $|A| f$ approaches the unity-gain frequency $g_m/(2\pi C_L)$. The simulator computes each point by a complex solve, not by this formula.

## The pole frequency

The pole is where $|A|$ is 3 dB below $|A_0|$ and the added phase is -45 degrees: $f_p = 1/(2\pi R_{out} C_L)$. Kilohms times picofarads is nanoseconds, so with $R_{out} = 33.3$ k$\Omega$ and $C_L = 2$ pF the time constant is 66.7 ns and $f_p = 2.39$ MHz. AC analysis also reveals what this one-pole model omits: the gate-drain capacitance couples input to output, creating a right-half-plane zero and, with a source resistance, a Miller-multiplied input pole. A pole-zero analysis finds these roots directly from the generalized eigenproblem of $G$ and $C$.

## Going deeper

label: Noise analysis
lesson:
# Noise analysis

Noise analysis is a small-signal frequency sweep with a twist: instead of one input, every resistor and transistor contributes a random noise source, and the simulator sums their powers at the output. Because the sources are uncorrelated, power densities add, not amplitudes. Simulators compute each source's transfer to the output with one adjoint solve per frequency, then report output noise and the equivalent noise referred to the input.

## Thermal noise of a resistor

A resistor at temperature $T$ has thermal noise modeled as a series voltage source with one-sided power spectral density $4kTR$ in V$^2$/Hz, or equivalently a parallel current source with density $4kT/R$. At 300 K, $4kT = 1.657 \times 10^{-20}$ J. For 1 k$\Omega$, $4kTR = 1.657 \times 10^{-17}$ V$^2$/Hz, and the density is its square root, 4.07 nV/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$. It scales as $\sqrt{R}$: 100 k$\Omega$ gives 40.7 nV/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$. Transistors add channel thermal noise, proportional to $g_m$, and flicker noise, whose density grows as $1/f$; the compact model supplies each density at the operating point.

## Summing independent noise at the output

Each source reaches the output through a transfer function $H_i(f)$, and uncorrelated sources add in power:
$$S_{out}(f) = \sum_i |H_i(f)|^2 S_i(f).$$
For a resistor contributing 4 nV/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ through a gain of 10 and a transistor contributing 3 nV/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ through a gain of 10, the output density is $\sqrt{40^2 + 30^2} = 50$ nV/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$, not 70. A simulator obtains all $H_i$ at once with an adjoint solve: one solve of $(G + j\omega C)^T \lambda = e_{out}$ per frequency gives the transfer from every possible source location. Dividing the output density by the signal gain gives the input-referred noise.

## Integrated kT/C noise

Integrating the output density over frequency gives the total rms noise. For a resistor across a capacitor, the density $4kTR$ shaped by the RC low-pass integrates to a variance of exactly $kT/C$, independent of $R$: a larger resistor is noisier but filters more, and the two effects cancel. At 300 K, 1 pF gives $\sqrt{kT/C} = \sqrt{4.14 \times 10^{-9}} = 64.4$ uV rms. This sets the noise floor of every sampling circuit and switched-capacitor stage, and it explains why sampling capacitors in high-resolution converters must be large. A noise analysis reproduces it only if its sweep covers the bandwidth well beyond the RC corner.

## Going deeper

Razavi, "Design of Analog CMOS Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., McGraw-Hill, 2017), chapter 7; Rohrer, Nagel, Meyer and Weber, "Computationally efficient electronic-circuit noise calculations" (IEEE JSSC, 1971).

label: Shooting for periodic steady state
lesson:
# Shooting for periodic steady state

Many circuits are judged in periodic steady state: oscillators, mixers, switching converters, clocked comparators. A plain transient must wait for start-up transients to die out, which for a high-Q circuit can take thousands of periods. Shooting methods instead solve directly for the initial state that repeats after one period, using Newton on a boundary-value problem whose function evaluation is one period of transient integration.

## The periodic boundary condition

Let $\phi_T(x_0)$ be the state reached by integrating the circuit for one period $T$ from the state $x_0$. Periodic steady state requires $\phi_T(x_0) = x_0$. For a linear circuit driven by a periodic source, the one-period map is affine: $\phi_T(x_0) = a x_0 + b$, where $a$ describes how the initial state decays over a period and $b$ is the response to the drive. The fixed point is $x_0 = b/(1 - a)$. With $a = 0.75$ and $b = 1$ V, $x_0 = 4$ V: starting there, the circuit repeats exactly. For a vector state, $a$ is the state-transition matrix and $x_0 = (I - A)^{-1} b$.

## One shooting Newton step

For a nonlinear circuit, apply Newton to $r(x_0) = \phi_T(x_0) - x_0 = 0$. The Jacobian is $\partial\phi_T/\partial x_0 - I$, the sensitivity of the final state to the initial state minus the identity. That sensitivity comes almost free: it is the product of the per-step Jacobians the transient already factored, propagated along the period. With $x_0 = 0.7$ V, $\phi_T(x_0) = 0.65$ V and $\phi' = 0.15$, the residual is -0.05, the derivative -0.85, and $x_1 = 0.7 - (-0.05)/(-0.85) = 0.641$ V. Each Newton iteration costs one period of transient plus the sensitivity, and a few iterations usually suffice.

## Why brute-force transient is slow

In plain transient the initial-condition error decays by the factor $a$ per period. A circuit that keeps 99.5% of its error each period, typical of a high-Q resonator, needs $N$ periods with $0.995^N \le \varepsilon/e_0$. For $e_0 = 0.5$ V and $\varepsilon = 1$ mV, $N \ge \ln(0.002)/\ln(0.995) = 1240$ periods. Shooting reaches the same state in a handful of Newton iterations, each one period long, because Newton removes the slow mode directly instead of waiting for it to decay. For large circuits the dense sensitivity matrix is avoided with matrix-free Krylov methods, which only need its products with vectors.

## Going deeper

Aprille and Trick, "Steady-state analysis of nonlinear circuits with periodic inputs" (Proceedings of the IEEE, 1972); Kundert, White and Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, "Steady-State Methods for Simulating Analog and Microwave Circuits" (Kluwer, 1990).

label: Harmonic balance
lesson:
# Harmonic balance

Harmonic balance (HB) finds the periodic steady state in the frequency domain. Each circuit unknown is represented by its Fourier coefficients up to some harmonic, linear elements are stamped harmonic by harmonic exactly as in AC analysis, and nonlinear devices are evaluated in the time domain and transformed back with FFTs. Newton then balances the currents at every harmonic. HB is the workhorse of RF simulation, especially for mildly nonlinear circuits with frequency-domain models.

## Unknowns in the frequency domain

Truncate each waveform to a DC term and harmonics 1 to $K$: $x(t) = X_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{K} (X^c_k \cos k\omega t + X^s_k \sin k\omega t)$. Each of the circuit's $N$ unknowns then carries $2K + 1$ real coefficients, so the HB system has $N(2K + 1)$ real unknowns. A 100-unknown circuit with 10 harmonics has 2100. Linear elements stamp $G + jk\omega C$ at each harmonic independently, but every nonlinear device couples all harmonics of its terminals, so the Jacobian is block-dense in the harmonic dimension. That is why large HB problems are solved with GMRES and preconditioners rather than direct LU.

## Harmonics of a quadratic nonlinearity

A nonlinear device generates harmonics of its drive. For $i = a_1 v + a_2 v^2$ with $v = A\cos\omega t$, the identity $\cos^2 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12\cos 2\omega t$ gives
$$i = \tfrac{a_2 A^2}{2} + a_1 A \cos\omega t + \tfrac{a_2 A^2}{2}\cos 2\omega t.$$
The quadratic term produces a DC shift and a second harmonic, each of amplitude $a_2 A^2/2$. With $a_1 = 3$ mS, $a_2 = 1.5$ mA/V$^2$ and $A = 0.2$ V, the fundamental is 0.6 mA and the DC and second harmonic are 0.03 mA. HB obtains these coefficients numerically: sample the waveform at $2K + 1$ or more points per period, evaluate the device, and FFT.

## Harmonics of a cubic nonlinearity

A cubic term $a_3 v^3$ uses $\cos^3 = \tfrac34\cos + \tfrac14\cos 3$:
$$i = \left(a_1 A + \tfrac34 a_3 A^3\right)\cos\omega t + \tfrac14 a_3 A^3 \cos 3\omega t.$$
With a negative $a_3$ the fundamental shrinks as the drive grows: gain compression. For $a_1 = 4.5$ mS, $a_3 = -0.1$ mA/V$^3$ and $A = 0.6$ V, the fundamental is $2.7 - 0.0162 = 2.684$ mA and the third harmonic is -0.0054 mA. With two input tones the same cubic term creates intermodulation products at $2f_1 - f_2$, which multitone HB captures directly. Truncating $K$ too low aliases the harmonics a strong nonlinearity generates, so HB suits mild nonlinearity best.

## Going deeper

Kundert, White and Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, "Steady-State Methods for Simulating Analog and Microwave Circuits" (Kluwer, 1990); Maas, "Nonlinear Microwave and RF Circuits" (2nd ed., Artech House, 2003).

label: RF simulation beyond periodic steady state
lesson:
# RF simulation beyond periodic steady state

Periodic steady state is the base on which RF simulation builds. Mixers, oscillators and switched circuits need small-signal and noise analyses that account for a large periodic drive, and multitone or modulated signals need methods that avoid simulating millions of carrier cycles. Knowing which analysis answers which question, and when shooting or harmonic balance is the better base, is the core of RF simulation practice.

## Periodic small-signal analyses

A mixer's small RF input sees a circuit whose operating point is modulated by the large local oscillator. Linearizing about the periodic steady state gives a linear time-varying system, which translates a small input at $f$ to outputs at $f + k f_{LO}$ for every harmonic $k$. Periodic AC (PAC) computes those conversion gains; periodic transfer-function analysis (PXF) uses an adjoint solve to get the transfer from many inputs and sidebands to one output; periodic noise (PNoise) handles cyclostationary noise, including noise folded from the image and other sidebands onto the output. All three linearize around the PSS solution, so a poorly converged PSS gives wrong gains and noise.

## Multitone and envelope methods

Two tones at 1.000 and 1.001 GHz beat with a 1 us period while the carrier period is 1 ns, so a transient must integrate a thousand fast cycles to see one beat. Multitone harmonic balance represents both tones and their mixing products $m f_1 + n f_2$ directly, truncated by total order; the number of frequencies, and the system size, grows roughly quadratically with the order. A modulated carrier whose envelope varies over microseconds suits envelope following instead: a periodic problem at the carrier is solved at each step of a slow time axis. Both methods exploit the separation of time scales that plain transient cannot.

## Choosing shooting or harmonic balance

Shooting integrates in time, so it handles sharp switching edges with adaptive steps and few unknowns, which suits switched-capacitor circuits, switching converters and hard-driven mixers. Harmonic balance works in frequency, so it stamps frequency-domain models such as S-parameters directly, represents distributed elements exactly at each harmonic, and handles mildly nonlinear circuits with few harmonics, which suits low-noise amplifiers and power amplifiers with package models. Strongly nonlinear waveforms need many harmonics in HB and become expensive. Autonomous oscillators need an extra unknown in either method: the period, fixed by a phase condition that removes the arbitrary time shift.

## Going deeper

Kundert, White and Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, "Steady-State Methods for Simulating Analog and Microwave Circuits" (Kluwer, 1990); Telichevesky, Kundert and White, "Efficient steady-state analysis based on matrix-free Krylov-subspace methods" (DAC, 1995).

label: Direct sensitivity analysis
lesson:
# Direct sensitivity analysis

Sensitivity analysis asks how much an output moves when a parameter moves. Simulators compute it exactly, without finite differences, by differentiating the circuit equations themselves and reusing the factorization of the nominal solve. Sensitivities feed optimization and sizing, statistical design and worst-case estimation, so they are one of the most reused quantities a simulator produces.

## Differentiating the circuit equations

Differentiate $G(p)\, x(p) = b$ with respect to a parameter $p$: $G\, \partial x/\partial p = -(\partial G/\partial p)\, x$. The matrix is the nominal $G$, already factored, so each parameter costs one forward and back substitution. For a divider with $V_1$ through $R_1$ into the output and $R_2$ to ground, $v_{out} = V_1 R_2/(R_1 + R_2)$, so
$$\frac{\partial v_{out}}{\partial R_1} = -\frac{V_1 R_2}{(R_1 + R_2)^2}, \qquad \frac{\partial v_{out}}{\partial R_2} = \frac{V_1 R_1}{(R_1 + R_2)^2}.$$
With $V_1 = 2$ V, $R_1 = 3$ k$\Omega$ and $R_2 = 1$ k$\Omega$, $\partial v_{out}/\partial R_1 = -2/16 = -0.125$ V/k$\Omega$, or -125 mV per k$\Omega$. This direct method is exact to rounding.

## Normalized sensitivity

Raw derivatives have units and depend on scale. The normalized sensitivity
$$S^{v}_{p} = \frac{p}{v}\frac{\partial v}{\partial p}$$
is the percent change in the output per percent change in the parameter. For the divider, $S^{v}_{R_1} = -R_1/(R_1 + R_2)$ and $S^{v}_{R_2} = R_1/(R_1 + R_2)$; with $R_1 = 3$ k$\Omega$ and $R_2 = 1$ k$\Omega$ these are -0.75 and 0.75. They sum to zero, as they must: scaling both resistors together leaves a ratio unchanged. Normalized sensitivities let a designer rank parameters by influence regardless of units, which is the first step in deciding which tolerances matter and which device to resize.

## First-order change estimate

A sensitivity predicts small changes linearly: $\Delta v \approx (\partial v/\partial p)\Delta p$. For the divider above, a 2% increase in $R_1$ is $\Delta R_1 = 0.06$ k$\Omega$, so $\Delta v_{out} \approx -0.125 \times 0.06 = -7.5$ mV. Equivalently, the normalized sensitivity times the percent change gives the percent output change: $-0.75 \times 2\% = -1.5\%$ of 0.5 V. The estimate degrades for large changes or strongly nonlinear circuits, where the second derivative matters. Worst-case and statistical methods combine many first-order terms, so their accuracy rests on the parameter changes being small enough for linearity to hold.

## Going deeper

Director and Rohrer, "The generalized adjoint network and network sensitivities" (IEEE Transactions on Circuit Theory, 1969); Najm, "Circuit Simulation" (Wiley, 2010), chapter on sensitivity.

label: Adjoint sensitivity
lesson:
# Adjoint sensitivity

When a circuit has many parameters and few outputs, the direct method's one solve per parameter becomes expensive. The adjoint method reverses the bookkeeping: one solve per output, with the transposed matrix, gives the sensitivity of that output to every parameter at once. It is the circuit-simulation ancestor of reverse-mode automatic differentiation and backpropagation.

## The adjoint solve

For an output $y = e^T x$, where $e$ selects the output node, solve the adjoint system
$$G^T \lambda = e.$$
The vector $\lambda$ is the response of every node to a unit current injected at the output in the transposed circuit. For a resistive network $G$ is symmetric, so $\lambda = G^{-1} e$. With $g_a$ from node 1 to ground, $g_b$ between nodes 1 and 2, $g_c$ from node 2 to ground and output $v_2$: $\lambda_1 = g_b/\det G$ and $\lambda_2 = (g_a + g_b)/\det G$. For $g_a = g_b = g_c = 1$ mS, $\det G = 3$, $\lambda_1 = 0.333$ k$\Omega$ and $\lambda_2 = 0.667$ k$\Omega$. The factors of $G$ are reused: solving with $G^T$ swaps the roles of $L$ and $U$.

## Sensitivity from two solutions

From the direct formula, $\partial y/\partial p = -e^T G^{-1}(\partial G/\partial p) x = -\lambda^T (\partial G/\partial p)\, x$. For a conductance $g$ between nodes $p$ and $q$, $\partial G/\partial g$ is the resistor stamp, so
$$\frac{\partial y}{\partial g} = -(\lambda_p - \lambda_q)(v_p - v_q),$$
with ground at 0. In the example with 1 mA into node 1, $v_1 = 0.667$ V and $v_2 = 0.333$ V. Then $\partial v_2/\partial g_b = -(0.333 - 0.667)(0.667 - 0.333) = 0.111$ V/mS: more conductance between the nodes raises the output. Every element's sensitivity is an inner product of the nominal and adjoint solutions at its terminals.

## Counting solves: direct versus adjoint

After the nominal factorization, the direct method needs one substitution per parameter and yields every output; the adjoint method needs one substitution per output and yields every parameter. With 300 parameters and 2 outputs, direct costs 300 solves and adjoint costs 2, each followed by cheap inner products. Optimization of a few performance metrics over many device sizes is therefore an adjoint problem. The same reasoning appears in noise analysis, which uses one adjoint solve per frequency to get every noise source's transfer to the output, and in transient adjoint sensitivity, which integrates backward in time and must store the forward trajectory.

## Going deeper

Director and Rohrer, "The generalized adjoint network and network sensitivities" (IEEE Transactions on Circuit Theory, 1969); Vlach and Singhal, "Computer Methods for Circuit Analysis and Design" (2nd ed., 1994).

label: Device mismatch and the Pelgrom model
lesson:
# Device mismatch and the Pelgrom model

Two transistors drawn identically, side by side, are never identical. Random dopant fluctuation, line-edge roughness and other local effects give each device its own threshold and current factor. This local mismatch sets the offset of comparators, the accuracy of current mirrors and the stability of SRAM cells. The Pelgrom model captures its scaling with one law: the standard deviation falls with the square root of gate area.

## Mismatch shrinks with area

Pelgrom's law states that the threshold difference between two identical devices has standard deviation
$$\sigma(\Delta V_T) = \frac{A_{VT}}{\sqrt{WL}},$$
where $A_{VT}$ is a process coefficient, typically a few mV um. Averaging local fluctuations over a larger gate reduces their effect, and since the fluctuations are independent per unit area, the variance falls as one over area. With $A_{VT} = 3$ mV um, $W = 2$ um and $L = 0.5$ um, $\sqrt{WL} = 1$ um and $\sigma(\Delta V_T) = 3$ mV. A similar law with a coefficient $A_\beta$ describes the relative mismatch of the current factor. Distance between devices adds a further term in the original model, which careful layout minimizes.

## Sizing for a mismatch target

Inverting the law gives the area required for a target: $WL \ge (A_{VT}/\sigma)^2$. With $A_{VT} = 3$ mV um and a target of 1 mV, $WL \ge 9$ um$^2$; at $W = 4$ um that means $L \ge 2.25$ um. Halving the mismatch quadruples the area, and with it the capacitance and power at a given speed. This square-law trade-off is why precision analog circuits are large and why techniques such as offset calibration, chopping and auto-zeroing exist. A sizing tool that ignores mismatch will shrink matched pairs until Monte Carlo reveals unacceptable offset, so mismatch belongs in the optimization from the start.

## Per-device sigma in a Monte Carlo model

Pelgrom's coefficient describes the difference of a pair. A Monte Carlo simulator instead draws an independent threshold shift for each device. The difference of two independent draws with standard deviation $\sigma_{dev}$ has variance $2\sigma_{dev}^2$, so the model must use
$$\sigma_{dev} = \frac{\sigma(\Delta V_T)}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{A_{VT}}{\sqrt{2WL}}.$$
For a pair with $\sigma(\Delta V_T) = 3$ mV, each device gets $\sigma_{dev} = 2.12$ mV. Putting the pair value on each device overstates mismatch by $\sqrt{2}$, and placing one random value on a shared model card makes all devices move together, which models global variation and gives zero mismatch. Foundry statistical models encode the correct per-instance draws.

## Going deeper

Pelgrom, Duinmaijer and Welbers, "Matching properties of MOS transistors" (IEEE JSSC, 1989); Kinget, "Device mismatch and tradeoffs in the design of analog circuits" (IEEE JSSC, 2005).

label: Corners and Monte Carlo in circuit simulation
prereqs: Device mismatch and the Pelgrom model
lesson:
# Corners and Monte Carlo in circuit simulation

Variation enters circuit simulation in two ways. Corner analysis runs the circuit at a few deliberately chosen parameter sets; Monte Carlo draws many random parameter sets from the statistical models and estimates distributions. Both multiply the number of simulations, so knowing exactly how their costs grow, and how their accuracy depends on the number of runs, is essential for planning verification and for building faster statistical methods.

## Counting corner runs

A corner is one combination of process corner (TT, FF, SS, FS, SF), supply voltage, temperature and parasitic-extraction corner. Corners multiply: 5 process corners, 3 supplies, 3 temperatures and 3 extraction corners give $5 \times 3 \times 3 \times 3 = 135$ runs per testbench, before Monte Carlo or multiple testbenches. That product is why teams prune corner lists per metric, choosing the corners known to bound each specification, and why simulators and farms schedule corner runs in parallel. Each run is an independent simulation, so corner analysis parallelizes perfectly, but its total cost grows multiplicatively with every new axis.

## Samples for a yield estimate

Monte Carlo estimates yield as the fraction of samples that pass. Each sample is a Bernoulli trial, so the estimate's standard error is $\sqrt{Y(1 - Y)/N}$. For a target standard error se, $N = Y(1 - Y)/\text{se}^2$. With $Y$ near 0.9 and se $= 0.01$, $N = 0.09/10^{-4} = 900$ samples. The required count does not depend on the number of random parameters, which is Monte Carlo's great strength in high dimension, but it grows as $1/\text{se}^2$. Verifying a very high yield, such as a failure rate of $10^{-6}$ per SRAM cell, would need millions of samples, which motivates importance sampling and other rare-event methods.

## Standard error of a simulated mean

For a continuous metric such as offset or delay, the sample mean of $N$ runs has standard error $\sigma/\sqrt{N}$, where $\sigma$ is the sample standard deviation. With $\sigma = 5$ mV over 100 runs, the mean is known to within 0.5 mV (one standard error). Quadrupling the runs halves the error. Note the difference between the spread of the metric, $\sigma$, which describes the circuit, and the standard error, which describes the estimate. A designer usually needs the spread, for example to check a $3\sigma$ limit, and the standard error tells how many runs make that estimate trustworthy.

## Going deeper

Rubinstein and Kroese, "Simulation and the Monte Carlo Method" (3rd ed., Wiley, 2016); Najm, "Circuit Simulation" (Wiley, 2010), chapter on statistical analysis.
