label: Process corners and what they bound
prereqs: Corners and Monte Carlo in circuit simulation
lesson:
# Process corners and what they bound

Process corners are the most used and most misused variation tool in circuit simulation. A corner is a shifted set of global process parameters that makes devices fast or slow. Corners are cheap and deterministic, but they bound only what they were built to bound. A tool designer must know what each corner models, which corner stresses which check, and which effects no global corner can capture.

## The named corners

Corner names list NMOS speed, then PMOS: TT is typical-typical, FF fast-fast, SS slow-slow, FS fast NMOS with slow PMOS, SF the reverse. Fast devices have lower threshold voltage and higher mobility, slow devices the opposite. Each corner is a model library section, selected with a line such as .lib models.lib ss, that shifts parameters for every device on the die together: it models global, die-to-die or wafer-to-wafer variation. The skewed corners FS and SF exist because some circuits fail when the two device types are unbalanced: inverter switching thresholds, ratioed logic and sense amplifiers depend on the NMOS-to-PMOS strength ratio.

## Which corner for which check

Each specification has a worst corner. Setup timing fails when paths are slow: SS devices at low supply and the slowest temperature. Hold timing and dynamic power are worst when devices are fast and supply is high: FF at high voltage. Leakage grows exponentially as thresholds drop and temperature rises, so it is worst at FF and high temperature. The slowest temperature is not always hot: in advanced low-voltage processes, cooling raises the threshold more than it improves mobility, so cold becomes slow, an effect called temperature inversion. A sign-off plan pairs each metric with the corners that bound it rather than running every corner for everything.

## What corners miss

Global corners shift matched devices together, so their difference stays zero: a comparator's offset passes every corner and still fails on silicon. Local mismatch needs Monte Carlo with per-device variation. Corners also bound parameters, not performance: a $\pm 3\sigma$ parameter corner pushes all parameters to extremes at once, which may be too pessimistic for one metric and not worst for another, because performance depends on many correlated parameters nonlinearly. Statistical or performance-specific corners, derived from a block's own Monte Carlo distribution, give sharper bounds. Reusing a digital library's SS and FF as the only checks for an analog reference misses its temperature and mismatch behavior entirely.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed., Addison-Wesley, 2010), chapter on variation; Pelgrom, Duinmaijer and Welbers, "Matching properties of MOS transistors" (IEEE JSSC, 1989).

label: Moments of an RC network
lesson:
# Moments of an RC network

Model order reduction for interconnect starts from moments: the coefficients of the Taylor expansion of a transfer function around $s = 0$. For RC networks the first moment is minus the Elmore delay, and higher moments follow from a simple recursion that reuses one factorization. Moments are cheap, they capture the low-frequency behavior that dominates delay, and they are what AWE and Krylov methods match.

## The first moment at the far end

Expand the transfer function from the driven root to node $i$ as $H_i(s) = m_0 + m_1 s + m_2 s^2 + \cdots$. For an RC tree driven by a voltage source, $m_0 = 1$ (at DC every node follows the source) and
$$m_1^{(i)} = -\sum_k R_{ik} C_k,$$
where $R_{ik}$ is the resistance shared by the paths from the root to $i$ and to $k$. This is minus the Elmore delay. For a chain of $R_1 = 100\ \Omega$ to node 1 with 20 fF and $R_2 = 200\ \Omega$ to node 2 with 10 fF, the far end has $m_1 = -(100 \cdot 20 + 300 \cdot 10)$ ohm fF $= -5000$ fs $= -5$ ps.

## The first moment at an inner node

At an inner node of a chain, capacitors beyond the node share only the resistance up to that node. At node 1 of the chain above, $C_1$ shares $R_1$ and so does $C_2$, so $m_1^{(1)} = -100(20 + 10) = -3000$ fs $= -3$ ps. The general computation is a linear solve: moments satisfy $G m_0 = b$ and $G m_q = -C m_{q-1}$, so $m_1 = -G^{-1} C m_0$. For a tree, $G^{-1}$ has the shared-resistance entries $R_{ik}$, and the recursion becomes two tree traversals: a post-order pass accumulating downstream capacitance and a pre-order pass accumulating resistance times downstream capacitance.

## The second moment

Higher moments reuse the same recursion with the previous moment as the excitation: $m_q = -G^{-1} C m_{q-1}$, so in a tree
$$m_2^{(i)} = -\sum_k R_{ik} C_k m_1^{(k)}.$$
Each capacitor is weighted by the first moment at its own node. In the chain above, $m_1^{(1)} = -3$ ps and $m_1^{(2)} = -5$ ps, so at node 2, $m_2 = 100 \cdot 20 \cdot 3 + 300 \cdot 10 \cdot 5 = 6000 + 15000 = 21000$ fs ps $= 21$ ps$^2$. Moments alternate in sign for RC trees. Each new moment costs one forward and back substitution with the factored $G$, which is why moment computation scales to huge parasitic networks.

## Going deeper

Pillage and Rohrer, "Asymptotic waveform evaluation for timing analysis" (IEEE TCAD, 1990); Pillage, Rohrer and Visweswariah, "Electronic Circuit and System Simulation Methods" (McGraw-Hill, 1995).

The transfer function to each node expands as $H(s) = m_0 + m_1 s + m_2 s^2 + \cdots$ with $m_0 = 1$. What is the first moment $m_1$ at the far end, node 3, in picoseconds? Round to 3 decimal places.

label: Asymptotic waveform evaluation
lesson:
# Asymptotic waveform evaluation

Asymptotic waveform evaluation (AWE) turns a handful of moments into a reduced model with a few poles. It matches the moments with a Pade approximation, a rational function whose expansion agrees with the computed moments, and reads the dominant poles and residues from it. AWE made interconnect delay calculation far more accurate than Elmore at little cost, and its numerical weaknesses motivated the Krylov methods that replaced it.

## A one-pole fit from two moments

The simplest model is one pole: $H(s) \approx k/(1 - s/p)$, whose expansion is $k(1 + s/p + s^2/p^2 + \cdots)$. Matching the first two moments gives $m_0 = k$ and $m_1 = k/p$, so
$$p = \frac{m_0}{m_1}.$$
For an RC tree, $m_1 < 0$, so the pole is negative, as a stable pole must be. With $m_0 = 1$ and $m_1 = -2.5$ ns, $p = -0.4$ 1/ns and the time constant is $-1/p = 2.5$ ns, exactly the Elmore delay. The one-pole AWE model is therefore Elmore's model written as a waveform, with the response $1 - e^{pt}$ to a unit step.

## Delay from the dominant pole

A single-pole step response $1 - e^{-t/\tau}$ crosses 50% at $t_{50} = \tau \ln 2 \approx 0.693\tau$. With $\tau = -m_1/m_0$, the one-pole model predicts $t_{50} = 0.693 \times$ Elmore delay. For $m_1 = -0.3$ ns, $t_{50} = 0.208$ ns. The Elmore value itself upper-bounds the true 50% delay of an RC tree. Near the driver, where resistive shielding makes the response far from single-pole, both estimates can be very pessimistic; at the far end of a distributed line, $\ln 2$ times Elmore gives 0.35 RC against a true value near 0.38 RC. Higher-order AWE models were introduced to remove such errors.

## A two-pole Pade fit

A two-pole model $(a_0 + a_1 s)/(1 + b_1 s + b_2 s^2)$ matches four moments. Multiplying out and matching the coefficients of $s^2$ and $s^3$ gives the linear system
$$\begin{pmatrix} m_0 & m_1 \\ m_1 & m_2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} b_2 \\ b_1 \end{pmatrix} = -\begin{pmatrix} m_2 \\ m_3 \end{pmatrix}.$$
By Cramer's rule $b_1 = (m_1 m_2 - m_0 m_3)/(m_0 m_2 - m_1^2)$. For a response with time constants 2 and 0.5 ns weighted 0.8 and 0.2, the moments are $1, -1.7, 3.25, -6.425$, and $b_1 = 0.9/0.36 = 2.5$ ns, the sum of the time constants; the poles are the roots of the denominator. With higher orders the moment matrix becomes ill-conditioned and the Pade model can return unstable poles, which PRIMA's projection avoids.

## Going deeper

Pillage and Rohrer, "Asymptotic waveform evaluation for timing analysis" (IEEE TCAD, 1990); Feldmann and Freund, "Efficient linear circuit analysis by Pade approximation via the Lanczos process" (IEEE TCAD, 1995).

label: PRIMA and passive reduction
prereqs: Model order reduction by Krylov projection
lesson:
# PRIMA and passive reduction

PRIMA reduces large linear RLC networks by projecting their MNA matrices onto a Krylov subspace. It matches moments like AWE, but implicitly and stably, through an orthonormal basis built by block Arnoldi, and its congruence projection preserves passivity. Post-layout parasitic networks with millions of elements are routinely reduced this way before simulation or timing analysis.

## Moments matched by a block Krylov basis

For an interconnect with $p$ ports, the moments of the port admittance are generated by the Krylov sequence $R, AR, A^2R, \ldots$ with $A = -G^{-1}C$ and $R = G^{-1}B$, where $B$ selects the ports. Block Arnoldi builds an orthonormal basis $V$ of this space, $p$ columns per iteration. A basis of $q$ columns, $q = mp$, matches the first $m = q/p$ block moments. An 8-port net reduced with $q = 48$ columns matches 6 block moments. Orthonormalization is what makes this stable where AWE fails: the basis vectors stay well separated instead of all aligning with the dominant eigenvector.

## Congruence projection

PRIMA projects the MNA matrices by congruence: $\hat{G} = V^T G V$, $\hat{C} = V^T C V$, $\hat{B} = V^T B$. For a two-node conductance matrix $G = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ mS and a single basis vector $v = (0.6, 0.8)$, $\hat{G} = 3 \cdot 0.36 - 2 \cdot 0.48 + 2 \cdot 0.64 = 1.4$ mS. When $G$ and $C$ are arranged so that their symmetric parts are positive semidefinite, which MNA allows for RLC networks, congruence preserves that property, and the reduced model is passive: it cannot generate energy, so connecting it to other passive circuits cannot create instability. Moment matching alone, as in AWE, gives no such guarantee.

## The reduced pole

A one-column reduction of an RC network has one state and one pole, $-\hat{G}/\hat{C}$. With $G$ as above and $C = \mathrm{diag}(1, 0.5)$ pF, $\hat{C} = 0.36 + 0.32 = 0.68$ pF and the pole is $-1.4/0.68 = -2.06$ 1/ns (millisiemens per picofarad is one per nanosecond). Because $\hat{G}$ and $\hat{C}$ are positive, the pole is always in the left half plane. In practice $q$ is chosen to cover the frequency band of interest, the reduced model is a small dense block stamped into MNA, and its order trades accuracy against the cost of that dense block.

## Going deeper

Odabasioglu, Celik and Pileggi, "PRIMA: passive reduced-order interconnect macromodeling algorithm" (IEEE TCAD, 1998); Antoulas, "Approximation of Large-Scale Dynamical Systems" (SIAM, 2005).

problems.e: Each block Krylov step adds one column per port, and q columns match $q/p = 48/8 = 6$ block moments.

problems.e: $v^T G v = 2 \cdot (-0.6)^2 + 2(-1)(-0.6)(0.8) + 2 \cdot (0.8)^2 = 2.96$ mS. Congruence keeps $\hat{G}$ positive definite when $G$ is, which preserves passivity.

problems.q: A two-node conductance matrix is $G = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ mS. PRIMA projects it with an orthonormal basis, here the single vector $v = (-0.6, 0.8)$, as $\hat{G} = v^T G v$. What is $\hat{G}$ in mS? Round to 4 decimal places.
problems.e: $v^T G v = 4 \cdot (-0.6)^2 + 2(-1)(-0.6)(0.8) + 1 \cdot (0.8)^2 = 3.04$ mS. Congruence keeps $\hat{G}$ positive definite when $G$ is, which preserves passivity.

problems.q: A two-node conductance matrix is $G = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -0.5 \\ -0.5 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ mS. PRIMA projects it with an orthonormal basis, here the single vector $v = (-0.6, 0.8)$, as $\hat{G} = v^T G v$. What is $\hat{G}$ in mS? Round to 4 decimal places.
problems.e: $v^T G v = 3 \cdot (-0.6)^2 + 2(-0.5)(-0.6)(0.8) + 4 \cdot (0.8)^2 = 4.12$ mS. Congruence keeps $\hat{G}$ positive definite when $G$ is, which preserves passivity.

problems.q: A two-node RC model has $G = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ mS and $C = \mathrm{diag}(0.5, 1)$ pF. It is reduced to one state with $v = (0.8, 0.6)$: $\hat{G} = v^T G v$, $\hat{C} = v^T C v$. What is the pole $-\hat{G}/\hat{C}$ of the reduced model, in 1/ns? Round to 4 decimal places.
problems.e: $\hat{G} = 1.12$ mS and $\hat{C} = 0.68$ pF, so the pole is $-1.12/0.68 = -1.6471$ 1/ns (mS per pF is 1/ns). Both reduced matrices stay positive, so the pole stays in the left half plane.

problems.q: A two-node RC model has $G = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ mS and $C = \mathrm{diag}(0.5, 0.5)$ pF. It is reduced to one state with $v = (0.6, 0.8)$: $\hat{G} = v^T G v$, $\hat{C} = v^T C v$. What is the pole $-\hat{G}/\hat{C}$ of the reduced model, in 1/ns? Round to 4 decimal places.
problems.e: $\hat{G} = 0.4$ mS and $\hat{C} = 0.5$ pF, so the pole is $-0.4/0.5 = -0.8$ 1/ns (mS per pF is 1/ns). Both reduced matrices stay positive, so the pole stays in the left half plane.

problems.q: A two-node RC model has $G = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -0.5 \\ -0.5 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ mS and $C = \mathrm{diag}(2, 0.5)$ pF. It is reduced to one state with $v = (-0.6, 0.8)$: $\hat{G} = v^T G v$, $\hat{C} = v^T C v$. What is the pole $-\hat{G}/\hat{C}$ of the reduced model, in 1/ns? Round to 4 decimal places.
problems.e: $\hat{G} = 2.12$ mS and $\hat{C} = 1.04$ pF, so the pole is $-2.12/1.04 = -2.0385$ 1/ns (mS per pF is 1/ns). Both reduced matrices stay positive, so the pole stays in the left half plane.

label: Behavioral macromodels
lesson:
# Behavioral macromodels

Not every block can be simulated at transistor level or reduced from an exact netlist. Packages and boards arrive as measured S-parameters; op-amps and regulators are replaced by behavioral models to speed system simulation. Macromodeling turns such data or abstractions into models a simulator can integrate. The engineering questions are always the same: is the model stable, passive and causal, and over what range is it valid?

## Rational fits of measured data

Tabulated frequency data define a time response only through convolution, which is costly at every step and sensitive to the measured band's limits. Vector fitting instead fits a rational function $H(s) \approx d + \sum_i r_i/(s - p_i)$ by iteratively relocating poles, giving a state-space model or an equivalent circuit that a simulator integrates directly. The fitted poles must lie in the left half plane: a pole with positive real part is a growing mode that makes transient diverge, so fitting algorithms flip or constrain such poles. Like a PRIMA model, a fitted model is stamped as a small dense block, because its states couple all ports.

## Passivity and causality

A model of a passive structure must itself be passive: for an admittance model, the Hermitian part of $Y(j\omega)$ must be positive semidefinite at every frequency. A stable but non-passive model can make an interconnection of stable parts oscillate, because it can supply energy. Passivity is checked by testing eigenvalues of the real part over frequency or with Hamiltonian-matrix tests, and enforced by small perturbations of the residues. Causality requires the impulse response to vanish before $t = 0$; band-limited or inconsistent data can produce acausal fits. PRIMA guarantees passivity by construction, through congruence; data-driven fits must check and enforce it.

## Behavioral models in a netlist

Behavioral macromodels, often written in Verilog-A, replace transistor-level blocks with equations: an op-amp as gain, a pole and output limits; a digital block as a table of supply current versus time for power-grid analysis. They run far faster, but they model only what they encode, so a fixed current signature does not respond to supply droop and a one-pole op-amp does not slew realistically. Numerically, behavioral code must keep currents, charges and their derivatives continuous: an abrupt if-statement creates a discontinuity that makes Newton oscillate and forces tiny steps. Every macromodel should state its validity range of temperature, load and frequency.

## Going deeper

Gustavsen and Semlyen, "Rational approximation of frequency domain responses by vector fitting" (IEEE Transactions on Power Delivery, 1999); Kundert and Zinke, "The Designer's Guide to Verilog-AMS" (Kluwer, 2004).

problems.q:
Why is a reduced or fitted model typically stamped as a small dense block in the MNA matrix?

A) SPICE cannot store sparse blocks

B) Its state variables couple all ports to each other, unlike the sparse local stamps of physical elements

C) Reduction always produces diagonal matrices

D) Dense blocks are required by Newton
problems.a: Its state variables couple all ports to each other, unlike the sparse local stamps of physical elements
problems.e: Projection mixes the original states, so the reduced G and C are dense. Keeping the order small keeps that dense block cheap.

problems.q:
A rational fit reproduces the data well but has a pole with positive real part. What happens in transient?

A) The simulator ignores that pole

B) Nothing; poles affect only AC

C) The fit becomes passive automatically

D) The model has a growing exponential mode and the simulation can diverge
problems.a: The model has a growing exponential mode and the simulation can diverge
problems.e: A right-half-plane pole is an unstable mode. Fitting algorithms flip or constrain poles to the left half plane to keep the model stable.

problems.q:
A package is characterized by measured S-parameters from 10 MHz to 20 GHz. What does vector fitting produce for the simulator?

A) A Monte Carlo distribution of the S-parameters

B) A single resistor and capacitor

C) A rational function in s, a sum of pole-residue terms, that can be realized as an equivalent circuit or state-space model

D) A lookup table indexed by time
problems.a: A rational function in s, a sum of pole-residue terms, that can be realized as an equivalent circuit or state-space model
problems.e: Vector fitting iteratively relocates poles to fit frequency data with a rational model, which transient simulators can integrate directly.

problems.q:
What property of PRIMA guarantees a passive reduced model for RLC interconnect?

A) A congruence projection of the MNA matrices in their passive form, which preserves positive (semi)definiteness

B) Using a Pade approximation

C) Fitting the poles by least squares

D) Matching more moments than AWE
problems.a: A congruence projection of the MNA matrices in their passive form, which preserves positive (semi)definiteness
problems.e: PRIMA reduces $V^T G V$ and $V^T C V$ directly. With the MNA matrices arranged so their symmetric parts are positive semidefinite, the projections inherit that and stay passive.

problems.q:
After vector fitting, an engineer checks passivity by testing the eigenvalues of the real part of the admittance at many frequencies. What fix follows if some are negative?

A) Delete the offending ports

B) Increase the simulator timestep

C) Switch to backward Euler

D) Passivity enforcement: perturb the residues minimally until the violations disappear
problems.a: Passivity enforcement: perturb the residues minimally until the violations disappear
problems.e: Passivity enforcement adjusts the model, usually the residues, with a small change that removes negative-resistance regions while keeping the fit accurate.

problems.q:
A fitted model of a passive interconnect is stable but generates energy at some frequencies. Why is that a problem when it is connected to other circuits?

A) A non-passive model can make an otherwise stable interconnection oscillate or blow up

B) It has no effect if each part is stable alone

C) It makes the matrix symmetric

D) It only changes the DC operating point
problems.a: A non-passive model can make an otherwise stable interconnection oscillate or blow up
problems.e: Stability of each block does not guarantee stability of the connection. Passivity does: a network of passive parts cannot create energy.

problems.q:
A Verilog-A model computes an output current with an if-statement that jumps abruptly at a threshold. What numerical problem can that cause?

A) A singular capacitance matrix

B) Loss of passivity in AC

C) Nothing, because Verilog-A smooths it

D) A discontinuous current and derivative that make Newton oscillate and force tiny timesteps
problems.a: A discontinuous current and derivative that make Newton oscillate and force tiny timesteps
problems.e: Simulators need continuous currents and charges with continuous derivatives. Behavioral models should use smooth transitions such as tanh or limited slopes.

problems.q:
A Verilog-A model computes an output current with an if-statement that jumps abruptly at a threshold. What numerical problem can that cause?

A) A singular capacitance matrix

B) A discontinuous current and derivative that make Newton oscillate and force tiny timesteps

C) Nothing, because Verilog-A smooths it

D) Loss of passivity in AC
problems.a: A discontinuous current and derivative that make Newton oscillate and force tiny timesteps
problems.e: Simulators need continuous currents and charges with continuous derivatives. Behavioral models should use smooth transitions such as tanh or limited slopes.

problems.q:
A large digital block is replaced by a table of its supply current versus time for a power-grid simulation. What kind of model is this?

A) A passive RC model

B) A behavioral current-source macromodel that ignores the block's internal response to supply droop

C) A full transistor model

D) A PRIMA-reduced model of the transistors
problems.a: A behavioral current-source macromodel that ignores the block's internal response to supply droop
problems.e: Current signatures make grid simulation tractable, but because they are fixed, they do not change when the droop slows the logic.

label: Fast SPICE partitioning and multirate
prereqs: Sparsity and structure of the MNA matrix
lesson:
# Fast SPICE partitioning and multirate

Fast SPICE engines simulate circuits with millions of transistors, far beyond what one global Newton solve per time point allows. They partition the circuit into weakly coupled blocks, step each block at its own rate, skip blocks that are not changing, and solve small matrices instead of one huge one. Each trick has a measurable payoff and a measurable risk, and estimating both is how a tool designer chooses among them.

## Multirate time stepping

A single-rate simulator steps the whole circuit at the step the fastest block needs. If blocks need steps $h_1, \ldots, h_B$ over a run of length $T$, single-rate work is $B \cdot T/h_{min}$ block solves, while multirate work is $\sum_i T/h_i$. With three blocks needing 10, 20 and 100 ps, the speedup is $3/(1 + 0.5 + 0.1) = 1.875$. Real circuits, with a few fast clock nets and many slow analog or idle digital nodes, have far larger spreads. The cost is coupling: a slow block's inputs from a fast block must be interpolated, and if the coupling is strong, interpolation errors feed back and the blocks must be iterated or re-solved.

## Latency and event-driven evaluation

Most of a large digital or memory circuit is idle at any instant. A latent block, whose inputs have not changed beyond a tolerance, need not be re-evaluated: its previous solution still holds. If $N$ partitions exist, $a$ are active per step, and checking a latent one costs a fraction $c$ of a full evaluation, the speedup is $N/(a + (N - a)c)$. With 2000 partitions, 20 active and $c = 0.05$, that is $2000/(20 + 99) = 16.8$. The check itself becomes the bottleneck as activity falls, which is why event-driven engines track changes by events rather than scanning every partition at every step.

## Partitioned matrix solves

Partitioning also shrinks the linear algebra. If each matrix were factored densely, with cost proportional to size cubed, a 3000-unknown circuit split into 12 blocks of 250 plus a 50-unknown interface system would cost $12 \cdot 250^3 + 50^3$ instead of $3000^3$, a ratio of about 144. Real circuit matrices are sparse, so the true gain is far smaller, but the structure is the same: blocks are factored independently, possibly in parallel, and the interface (a Schur complement or a set of boundary variables) couples them. A large interface erases the gain, so partitioners cut where coupling is weak, typically at MOSFET gates, which draw no DC current.

## Going deeper

Najm, "Circuit Simulation" (Wiley, 2010), chapter on fast simulation; White and Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, "Relaxation Techniques for the Simulation of VLSI Circuits" (Kluwer, 1987).

problems.q: A fast SPICE engine partitions a circuit into 3 blocks of similar cost whose accuracy needs steps of 50 ps, 100 ps, 5 ps respectively. A single-rate simulator steps every block at the smallest step; a multirate one steps each block at its own. What speedup in block solves does multirate give over a fixed run time? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Single-rate work is $3 \cdot T/h_{min}$ and multirate work is $\sum T/h_i$. Their ratio is $3 / 1.15 = 2.61$, ignoring the cost of interpolating signals between blocks.

problems.q: A fast SPICE engine partitions a circuit into 2 blocks of similar cost whose accuracy needs steps of 100 ps, 2 ps respectively. A single-rate simulator steps every block at the smallest step; a multirate one steps each block at its own. What speedup in block solves does multirate give over a fixed run time? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Single-rate work is $2 \cdot T/h_{min}$ and multirate work is $\sum T/h_i$. Their ratio is $2 / 1.02 = 1.96$, ignoring the cost of interpolating signals between blocks.

problems.q: A fast SPICE engine partitions a circuit into 3 blocks of similar cost whose accuracy needs steps of 1 ps, 100 ps, 10 ps respectively. A single-rate simulator steps every block at the smallest step; a multirate one steps each block at its own. What speedup in block solves does multirate give over a fixed run time? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Single-rate work is $3 \cdot T/h_{min}$ and multirate work is $\sum T/h_i$. Their ratio is $3 / 1.11 = 2.7$, ignoring the cost of interpolating signals between blocks.

problems.q: Of 10000 partitions, on average 50 are active at each timestep; the rest are latent. Fully evaluating a partition costs 1 unit, and checking that a latent partition's inputs have not changed costs 0.02 units. What speedup does skipping latent partitions give over evaluating all of them? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Work per step drops from 10000 to $50 + 9950 \times 0.02 = 249$ units, a speedup of 40.16.

problems.q: Of 1000 partitions, on average 50 are active at each timestep; the rest are latent. Fully evaluating a partition costs 1 unit, and checking that a latent partition's inputs have not changed costs 0.02 units. What speedup does skipping latent partitions give over evaluating all of them? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Work per step drops from 1000 to $50 + 950 \times 0.02 = 69$ units, a speedup of 14.49.

problems.q: Of 5000 partitions, on average 500 are active at each timestep; the rest are latent. Fully evaluating a partition costs 1 unit, and checking that a latent partition's inputs have not changed costs 0.05 units. What speedup does skipping latent partitions give over evaluating all of them? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Work per step drops from 5000 to $500 + 4500 \times 0.05 = 725$ units, a speedup of 6.9.

problems.q: Suppose each matrix were factored as dense, with cost proportional to size cubed. A 6000-unknown circuit is split into 12 equal blocks plus a 100-unknown interface system solved after them. What is the ratio of the unpartitioned cost to the partitioned cost? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $6000^3$ against $12 \cdot 500^3 + 100^3$: the ratio is 143.9. Real circuit matrices are sparse, so true gains are smaller, but the interface size still bounds the benefit.

problems.q: Suppose each matrix were factored as dense, with cost proportional to size cubed. A 6000-unknown circuit is split into 4 equal blocks plus a 100-unknown interface system solved after them. What is the ratio of the unpartitioned cost to the partitioned cost? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $6000^3$ against $4 \cdot 1500^3 + 100^3$: the ratio is 16. Real circuit matrices are sparse, so true gains are smaller, but the interface size still bounds the benefit.

problems.q: Suppose each matrix were factored as dense, with cost proportional to size cubed. A 2400-unknown circuit is split into 6 equal blocks plus a 100-unknown interface system solved after them. What is the ratio of the unpartitioned cost to the partitioned cost? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $2400^3$ against $6 \cdot 400^3 + 100^3$: the ratio is 35.9. Real circuit matrices are sparse, so true gains are smaller, but the interface size still bounds the benefit.

label: Table models and fast SPICE accuracy
prereqs: Linearizing a MOSFET at a Newton iterate
lesson:
# Table models and fast SPICE accuracy

Besides partitioning, fast SPICE engines save time by simplifying what they evaluate: table models in place of compact models, relaxed tolerances on digital-like blocks, reuse of identical subcircuit solutions, and reduced parasitic networks. These choices are why full-chip transistor-level simulation is possible at all, and also why its results must be trusted selectively. The designer's skill is knowing when the fast answer is good enough and when to recurse into accurate SPICE.

## Replacing compact models with tables

A BSIM-class model evaluates long sequences of equations per device per Newton iteration. A table model precomputes currents and charges on a grid of terminal voltages and interpolates, costing a few multiply-adds. Interpolation must keep derivatives continuous: piecewise-linear tables have piecewise-constant conductances that jump at grid lines, which makes Newton oscillate across them, so engines use splines or other smooth schemes. A table is valid only where it was built: other temperatures, geometries or corners need their own tables or extra dimensions. Grid resolution trades memory and build time against accuracy, and the subthreshold region, where current changes by decades over a few hundred millivolts, is the hardest to resolve.

## Relaxed tolerances and reuse

Digital partitions swing rail to rail, so millivolt errors rarely change edge timing or power, and fast engines relax Newton and step tolerances there. Memory arrays contain thousands of identical cells in identical states; isomorphism detection solves one and reuses the result for all with the same boundary conditions. Post-layout netlists carry millions of parasitic resistors and capacitors, which are reduced before simulation by node elimination or moment-matching projection, keeping delay behavior with far fewer elements. These choices are bundled into accuracy or speed modes, so a single setting moves tolerances, table resolution and partitioning aggressiveness together, which is a classic Tier 1 control for a user or an agent.

## When fast SPICE is not enough

Fast SPICE suits full-chip power, digital timing of custom blocks and functional checks of large mixed designs. It is the wrong tool where the answer depends on small differences: comparator offset to 0.1 mV, leakage of a sleeping memory, distortion of an analog front end, or the stability of a tightly coupled feedback loop that a partitioner may cut and treat as weak. The productive practice is two-level: run the fast engine broadly, then recurse into accurate SPICE on the few blocks or paths where the fast engine's error budget could change a decision. Sign-off of precision analog metrics stays on accurate simulation.

## Going deeper

Najm, "Circuit Simulation" (Wiley, 2010), chapter on fast simulation; Rabbat, Sangiovanni-Vincentelli and Hsieh, "A multilevel Newton algorithm with macromodeling and latency for the analysis of large-scale nonlinear circuits in the time domain" (IEEE TCAS, 1979).

problems.q:
A table model is built from SPICE runs at one temperature. What must the fast simulator do for another temperature?

A) Use another table (or an extra table dimension) built at that temperature

B) Reuse the table and rely on gmin

C) Nothing, since tables are temperature independent

D) Scale every current by the absolute temperature ratio
problems.a: Use another table (or an extra table dimension) built at that temperature
problems.e: Device behavior depends on temperature through mobility, threshold and more. A table is only valid where it was characterized.

problems.q:
A table model is built from SPICE runs at one temperature. What must the fast simulator do for another temperature?

A) Nothing, since tables are temperature independent

B) Reuse the table and rely on gmin

C) Scale every current by the absolute temperature ratio

D) Use another table (or an extra table dimension) built at that temperature
problems.a: Use another table (or an extra table dimension) built at that temperature
problems.e: Device behavior depends on temperature through mobility, threshold and more. A table is only valid where it was characterized.

problems.q:
Why do table models often use smooth splines rather than linear interpolation?

A) Linear interpolation cannot be stored

B) Splines need less memory

C) Splines are exact for BSIM

D) Continuous first derivatives give continuous conductances, which Newton and small-signal analysis need
problems.a: Continuous first derivatives give continuous conductances, which Newton and small-signal analysis need
problems.e: A cubic spline is continuous with continuous first derivative, so the stamped conductances vary smoothly with bias.

problems.q:
A fast SPICE run and a SPICE run differ by 3% in the delay of a critical path. Which knob most directly trades this accuracy against runtime?

A) The number of .print statements

B) The netlist node names

C) The output file format

D) The accuracy level or speed mode, which sets tolerances, table resolution and partitioning aggressiveness
problems.a: The accuracy level or speed mode, which sets tolerances, table resolution and partitioning aggressiveness
problems.e: Fast SPICE tools expose modes that bundle tolerances and model choices. Moving toward accuracy shrinks the error at higher cost.

problems.q:
Fast SPICE tools relax Newton and timestep tolerances on digital-like partitions. Why is this often acceptable there?

A) Digital nodes swing rail to rail, so small voltage errors rarely change logic timing or power much

B) Digital partitions are never stiff

C) Relaxed tolerances make results exact

D) Digital nodes have no capacitance
problems.a: Digital nodes swing rail to rail, so small voltage errors rarely change logic timing or power much
problems.e: The useful output of a digital partition is edge timing and current. Errors of a few millivolts are small compared with the swing.

problems.q:
A post-layout netlist has millions of parasitic resistors and capacitors. What does a fast simulator typically do before simulation?

A) Simulate them with fixed steps of one femtosecond

B) Convert them to inductors

C) Reduce the RC networks to smaller equivalents that preserve their low-frequency behavior

D) Remove all parasitics
problems.a: Reduce the RC networks to smaller equivalents that preserve their low-frequency behavior
problems.e: RC reduction, by node elimination or moment-matching projection, shrinks the parasitic network while keeping its delay behavior.

problems.q:
Leakage current of a sleeping SRAM is the sign-off metric. What risk does a table-based fast model carry?

A) Leakage cannot be computed at all

B) Leakage is independent of the device model

C) Tables always overestimate leakage by exactly 2x

D) Subthreshold currents are tiny and exponential, so table interpolation errors can be large in relative terms
problems.a: Subthreshold currents are tiny and exponential, so table interpolation errors can be large in relative terms
problems.e: Tables tuned for on-current accuracy can be poorly resolved in the subthreshold region, where currents change by decades over a few hundred millivolts.

problems.q:
A fast SPICE engine's partitioner splits a tightly coupled analog feedback loop across two partitions with relaxed coupling. What can go wrong?

A) The netlist cannot be parsed

B) The DC point becomes exact

C) Nothing, since partitions are always exact

D) The loop dynamics, such as its stability, are distorted because the coupling is treated as weak
problems.a: The loop dynamics, such as its stability, are distorted because the coupling is treated as weak
problems.e: Partitioned methods work well when coupling between partitions is weak or unidirectional. Strong bidirectional feedback across a boundary needs a joint solve.

problems.q:
A team wants the input offset of a comparator to within 0.1 mV. Should they use a fast SPICE mode?

A) Only with gmin stepping

B) Yes, if the clock is fast

C) Yes: fast SPICE is designed for offset

D) No: offset depends on small differences in device currents that table models and relaxed tolerances blur
problems.a: No: offset depends on small differences in device currents that table models and relaxed tolerances blur
problems.e: Precision analog metrics need accurate device models and tight tolerances. Fast SPICE suits large digital and mixed blocks where small analog errors do not matter.

label: Mixed-signal simulation and co-simulation
lesson:
# Mixed-signal simulation and co-simulation

Mixed-signal simulation runs an analog solver and an event-driven digital simulator together on one design. The two engines think in different currencies, continuous voltages and discrete events, and in different notions of time, adaptive steps and event queues. Making them agree at every boundary and at every instant is the whole problem, and its solutions recur in every co-simulation, from RTL with SPICE to chip with package.

## Crossing the analog-digital boundary

Where an analog net drives a digital input, an A-to-D connect module decides when the voltage counts as 0, 1 or unknown, usually with two thresholds (hysteresis) so that noise on a slow edge does not produce a burst of spurious events. Where a digital output drives an analog net, a D-to-A module presents a voltage or current source with finite rise time and output resistance, because an ideal step would be both unphysical and a numerical discontinuity. Connect modules are inserted automatically where nets of different disciplines meet. Their thresholds, rise times and impedances change event timing, so they are part of the model, not plumbing.

## Synchronizing two engines

A digital event that changes an analog source must land on an analog time point, so it becomes a breakpoint for the analog solver. In the other direction, an analog waveform may cross a threshold inside a step; the crossing is located by interpolation or bisection, the analog side backs up or cuts its step, and the digital engine is notified at the crossing time. In lockstep schemes neither engine advances past the next point where it might need input from the other. Waveform relaxation instead lets each subsystem simulate a whole window from the other's previous waveform and iterates, which converges quickly when coupling is weak or one-directional.

## Co-simulation architectures

In RTL-with-SPICE co-simulation, the analog engine usually dominates runtime, since it solves Newton systems at small steps while the digital side processes events cheaply. Real-number models move analog behavior into the digital simulator as discrete-time real values passed as events, trading fidelity for orders of magnitude in speed in chip-level regressions. ngspice's XSPICE extension provides event-driven code models, including digital ones, inside the analog simulator. When a co-simulation disagrees with an all-SPICE reference by an event, suspect the interface thresholds first, because they decide when the analog waveform becomes a logic transition.

## Going deeper

Kundert and Zinke, "The Designer's Guide to Verilog-AMS" (Kluwer, 2004); the ngspice manual, chapters on XSPICE code models.

problems.q:
A digital output drives an analog node. What should the D-to-A interface present to the analog solver?

A) Nothing; the analog node keeps its old voltage

B) A voltage or current source with finite rise time and output resistance

C) An ideal voltage step with zero rise time

D) A logic value stamped into the MNA matrix
problems.a: A voltage or current source with finite rise time and output resistance
problems.e: Ideal steps create discontinuities that the analog solver handles badly. A finite slope and impedance give a well-posed, realistic drive.

problems.q:
A digital output drives an analog node. What should the D-to-A interface present to the analog solver?

A) A logic value stamped into the MNA matrix

B) An ideal voltage step with zero rise time

C) Nothing; the analog node keeps its old voltage

D) A voltage or current source with finite rise time and output resistance
problems.a: A voltage or current source with finite rise time and output resistance
problems.e: Ideal steps create discontinuities that the analog solver handles badly. A finite slope and impedance give a well-posed, realistic drive.

problems.q:
An analog node drives a digital gate input in a mixed-signal simulation. What converts the analog waveform into a logic value?

A) A connect module (an A-to-D interface) with thresholds, often with hysteresis

B) The analog solver rounds the voltage to 0 or 1

C) A DC operating point at each clock edge

D) The digital simulator samples the node at every analog timestep
problems.a: A connect module (an A-to-D interface) with thresholds, often with hysteresis
problems.e: Connect modules define when an analog voltage counts as 0, 1 or X, typically with separate rising and falling thresholds to avoid chatter.

problems.q:
The digital engine schedules an event at 12.3 ns that changes an analog source. What must the analog solver do?

A) Restart from the DC operating point

B) Ignore it until the next accepted step

C) Place a breakpoint at 12.3 ns so its time grid hits the event exactly

D) Halve all future timesteps
problems.a: Place a breakpoint at 12.3 ns so its time grid hits the event exactly
problems.e: Digital events act like source corners for the analog side. Treating them as breakpoints keeps the discontinuity aligned with a time point.

problems.q:
The digital engine schedules an event at 12.3 ns that changes an analog source. What must the analog solver do?

A) Ignore it until the next accepted step

B) Halve all future timesteps

C) Place a breakpoint at 12.3 ns so its time grid hits the event exactly

D) Restart from the DC operating point
problems.a: Place a breakpoint at 12.3 ns so its time grid hits the event exactly
problems.e: Digital events act like source corners for the analog side. Treating them as breakpoints keeps the discontinuity aligned with a time point.

problems.q:
In lockstep synchronization, how do the analog and digital engines advance?

A) The digital engine always waits for the analog to finish

B) Neither advances past the next point where it may need input from the other

C) They exchange data only at the end

D) Each runs the entire simulation independently and the results are merged
problems.a: Neither advances past the next point where it may need input from the other
problems.e: Lockstep keeps both engines at consistent times, advancing to the next event or analog time point, which is safe but limits each engine's step choice.

problems.q:
A verification team co-simulates an RTL testbench in a digital simulator with an analog block in a SPICE engine. Where does most runtime typically go?

A) Parsing the netlists

B) The interface modules

C) The digital engine, because RTL is slower than SPICE

D) The analog engine, which solves nonlinear systems at small timesteps while the digital side processes events cheaply
problems.a: The analog engine, which solves nonlinear systems at small timesteps while the digital side processes events cheaply
problems.e: Event-driven RTL simulation is fast per event. The analog part pays for Newton solves at every time point, so its size and accuracy dominate the cost.

problems.q:
ngspice includes XSPICE. What does XSPICE add to the simulator?

A) Code models, including event-driven digital models, that run alongside the analog circuit

B) A layout extractor

C) A GPU solver

D) A harmonic-balance engine
problems.a: Code models, including event-driven digital models, that run alongside the analog circuit
problems.e: XSPICE extends SPICE with user-definable code models and an event-driven algorithm for digital and mixed-mode simulation.

problems.q:
ngspice includes XSPICE. What does XSPICE add to the simulator?

A) Code models, including event-driven digital models, that run alongside the analog circuit

B) A GPU solver

C) A layout extractor

D) A harmonic-balance engine
problems.a: Code models, including event-driven digital models, that run alongside the analog circuit
problems.e: XSPICE extends SPICE with user-definable code models and an event-driven algorithm for digital and mixed-mode simulation.

label: An agent that debugs convergence
prereqs: Running decks in ngspice and Xyce
lesson:
# An agent that debugs convergence

Convergence debugging is the simulator task most likely to be handed to an agent: it is frequent, tedious and full of patterns. An agent reads the simulator's log, classifies the failure, proposes the smallest change, reruns the deck and repeats in a harness loop. The hard part is not making the deck run, which loosening tolerances always achieves, but proving the fix did not change the answer.

## Reading the failure

A useful agent starts from the simulator's own diagnosis. A singular matrix naming a node points to topology: the node has no DC path, touching only capacitors or gates. A DC iteration limit with oscillating iterates points to nonlinearity or multiple solutions. Timestep-too-small at 3.2 ns points to a discontinuity, a model kink or a stiff event near that time, and the agent must extract which nodes were changing fastest and which source edge occurs there. Partial convergence, such as gmin stepping that stopped at $10^{-9}$ S, is a failure, not a result. Classification determines which knobs are relevant and keeps the agent from trying every option blindly.

## Proposing the smallest fix

The agent edits at the smallest safe tier, preferring changes to the path over changes to the equations. A .nodeset steers Newton without altering the circuit; a realistic rise time on an ideal PWL corner removes an unphysical discontinuity; a targeted initial condition kicks an oscillator. Raising reltol or setting a large global gmin also makes decks run, but they change accuracy or the circuit itself, so the harness should reject them unless the request explicitly trades accuracy. Editing a device model's equations is a core change and never a convergence fix. Each attempt's new failure message goes back to the model as feedback for the next proposal.

## Proving the fix did not change the answer

A converged run is evidence only that the simulator finished. The agent must compare key results, such as operating-point voltages, delays or gains, against a trusted reference or golden values within tolerance. To show a glitch was numerical, rerun at tighter tolerances and smaller steps: numerical artifacts change, physical behavior converges. When a circuit has several valid DC solutions, a nodeset that selects one must be reported as a choice, not hidden. A reward of 'the run finished' is easy to game by loosening tolerances or adding gmin until anything runs, so a tool-grounded reward must include agreement with golden results and penalize changes that alter the circuit.

## Going deeper

The ngspice manual, sections on convergence and options; Najm, "Circuit Simulation" (Wiley, 2010), chapters 4 and 5.

problems.q:
An agent sees that the operating point converged only after gmin stepping reduced gmin to 1e-9 S and then stopped. What does that report mean?

A) Gmin stepping is unnecessary in this deck

B) The DC point is exact and only transient remains

C) The operating point at the requested final gmin was not reached, so the result is not valid yet

D) The deck is solved and the result is reliable
problems.a: The operating point at the requested final gmin was not reached, so the result is not valid yet
problems.e: Intermediate gmin solutions are of a modified circuit. The agent must recognize partial convergence as a failure, not a success.

problems.q:
A transient fails with 'timestep too small' at 3.2 ns. Which information should the agent extract before proposing anything?

A) The number of comment lines

B) The final value of every node at the stop time

C) Only the total run time

D) Which nodes or devices were changing fastest or failing Newton near 3.2 ns, and what source edge happens there
problems.a: Which nodes or devices were changing fastest or failing Newton near 3.2 ns, and what source edge happens there
problems.e: Timestep failures are local in time and space. The agent needs the offending nodes and the event that triggered them to choose a targeted fix.

problems.q:
An agent sees that the operating point converged only after gmin stepping reduced gmin to 1e-9 S and then stopped. What does that report mean?

A) The operating point at the requested final gmin was not reached, so the result is not valid yet

B) The DC point is exact and only transient remains

C) The deck is solved and the result is reliable

D) Gmin stepping is unnecessary in this deck
problems.a: The operating point at the requested final gmin was not reached, so the result is not valid yet
problems.e: Intermediate gmin solutions are of a modified circuit. The agent must recognize partial convergence as a failure, not a success.

problems.q:
An agent proposes .options gmin=1e-6 to make a deck converge. Why should the harness reject this change?

A) It slows the simulation

B) A large permanent gmin changes the circuit being solved and corrupts high-impedance nodes

C) It has no effect on DC

D) gmin cannot be set in an options card
problems.a: A large permanent gmin changes the circuit being solved and corrupts high-impedance nodes
problems.e: Some fixes make convergence easier by solving a different problem. The harness must catch changes that alter the answer, not just the path to it.

problems.q:
A transient fails at a PWL source corner with zero rise time. What fix fits the smallest-change rule?

A) Give the corner a small finite rise time consistent with the real driver

B) Switch every device to a level-1 model

C) Delete the source

D) Set reltol to 0.1
problems.a: Give the corner a small finite rise time consistent with the real driver
problems.e: An ideal step is unphysical and creates a discontinuity. A realistic edge removes the cause without loosening global tolerances.

problems.q:
An agent can fix a DC convergence failure by adding .nodeset v(out)=1.2, by raising reltol to 1e-2, or by editing the diode model's equations. Which should it propose first?

A) The .nodeset: the smallest change that leaves tolerances and models intact

B) Editing the diode model

C) All three at once

D) Raising reltol, because it always works
problems.a: The .nodeset: the smallest change that leaves tolerances and models intact
problems.e: The agent edits at the smallest safe tier. A nodeset changes only the starting guess, so a converged answer still satisfies the original equations.

problems.q:
After a convergence fix, the deck runs. What must the agent check before reporting success?

A) That key results agree with a trusted reference run or golden values within tolerance

B) Only that the simulator returned exit code zero

C) That the run took less time

D) That the log is shorter
problems.a: That key results agree with a trusted reference run or golden values within tolerance
problems.e: A deck can converge to the wrong solution or with loosened accuracy. Comparison against golden results proves the fix did not change the answer.

problems.q:
A reward for a convergence-fixing agent is 'the simulator finished without error'. How can an agent game it?

A) By using fewer nodes

B) By loosening tolerances or adding gmin until anything runs, regardless of accuracy

C) By making the deck longer

D) It cannot be gamed
problems.a: By loosening tolerances or adding gmin until anything runs, regardless of accuracy
problems.e: A pass-or-fail reward ignores correctness. The reward must also include agreement with golden results and penalties for changes that alter the circuit.

problems.q:
An agent tightened reltol from 1e-3 to 1e-4 to remove a glitch, and the run passed. What differential check shows the glitch was numerical?

A) The waveform converges as tolerances tighten, while the glitch disappears; a physical glitch would persist

B) The run time doubled

C) The log has no warnings

D) The glitch moved to a later time
problems.a: The waveform converges as tolerances tighten, while the glitch disappears; a physical glitch would persist
problems.e: Numerical artifacts change with tolerances and step size; physical behavior converges to a limit. Comparing runs at several accuracies separates the two.

label: Simulator changes by tier
prereqs: Running decks in ngspice and Xyce
lesson:
# Simulator changes by tier

A SPICE-class simulator splits cleanly into the four engine layers. The immutable core is the numerical kernel: MNA assembly, sparse LU, Newton and the time loop. Policies are the integration methods and convergence strategies. Parameters are the options card. Hooks are the probes and measurements an agent reads. Assigning each change request to the smallest tier that can serve it is what keeps the kernel small and the change cheap.

## Options are Tier 1

Most simulator requests are configuration. Faster with some loss of accuracy: change reltol, trtol or the accuracy mode. Less ringing: method=gear with a chosen maximum order. Runs at five temperatures and three supplies: sweep settings in the deck. A tighter current tolerance for a low-power circuit: abstol. None of these recompiles anything; each is a reviewable one-line diff that is trivially reverted. The agent's first question for any request is whether an option already expresses it. Options still need verification, because a tolerance change moves results everywhere, but the verification is a rerun against golden values, not a code review.

## Plug-ins at the device and integrator seams

When no option suffices, the change belongs at an extension point. A proprietary transistor model enters at the device-model interface, often compiled from Verilog-A, without touching the solver. A custom convergence strategy, such as ramping supplies in a fixed order, belongs behind an operating-point homotopy interface. A new integrator needs a seam that lets it supply companion coefficients and its own error estimate and order, so step control keeps working. Seams should be coarse: a device plug-in called once per device per iteration through a virtual call can be dominated by call overhead, so batching devices of one model per call lets the plug-in vectorize and keeps the hot loop fast.

## Core edits to the solver

Tier 3 changes touch the numerical kernel: how the sparse matrix is ordered and factored, how Newton tests convergence, how the time loop accepts steps. They affect every simulation, so they require a human-approved diff and the full golden regression with QoR comparison on reference decks. A stream of Tier 3 requests for the same kind of change signals a missing seam: the varying behavior should move behind an extension point. When an agent proposes a core edit, such as a device equation written into the matrix assembly loop, the harness should steer it to the lower tier that can host the same behavior, here the device-model interface.

## Going deeper

The ngspice and Xyce documentation on options and device interfaces; McAndrew et al., "Best practices for compact modeling in Verilog-A" (IEEE Journal of the Electron Devices Society, 2015).

problems.q:
A user wants a deck to run with Gear integration of order 2 instead of trapezoidal. What kind of change is this?

A) A new device model

B) A configuration change through simulator options

C) A core rewrite of the time loop

D) A netlist topology change
problems.a: A configuration change through simulator options
problems.e: Simulators expose the integration method and maximum order as options, so choosing among built-in methods is Tier 1.

problems.q:
A user wants a deck to run with Gear integration of order 2 instead of trapezoidal. What kind of change is this?

A) A core rewrite of the time loop

B) A new device model

C) A netlist topology change

D) A configuration change through simulator options
problems.a: A configuration change through simulator options
problems.e: Simulators expose the integration method and maximum order as options, so choosing among built-in methods is Tier 1.

problems.q:
A user wants a deck to run with Gear integration of order 2 instead of trapezoidal. What kind of change is this?

A) A netlist topology change

B) A configuration change through simulator options

C) A core rewrite of the time loop

D) A new device model
problems.a: A configuration change through simulator options
problems.e: Simulators expose the integration method and maximum order as options, so choosing among built-in methods is Tier 1.

problems.q:
A device plug-in is called once per device per Newton iteration through a virtual call. A profile shows the call overhead dominates for millions of tiny devices. What design fixes it?

A) Remove derivatives from the interface

B) Call the plug-in once per run

C) Inline the plug-in into the netlist

D) A coarser seam: evaluate devices of one model in batches per call
problems.a: A coarser seam: evaluate devices of one model in batches per call
problems.e: Coarse plug-in calls amortize overhead and let the plug-in vectorize over many devices, keeping the hot loop efficient.

problems.q:
A team needs a proprietary transistor model that is not in the simulator. Where should it enter?

A) Tier 2: as a device plug-in at the device-model interface, for example compiled from Verilog-A

B) By editing every netlist

C) Tier 3: by editing the Newton loop

D) Tier 1: as an options card
problems.a: Tier 2: as a device plug-in at the device-model interface, for example compiled from Verilog-A
problems.e: Device models are the classic extension point. A plug-in supplies currents, charges and derivatives without touching the solver core.

problems.q:
A customer wants a custom convergence aid: ramp only the supply sources in a fixed order. What is the right tier and seam?

A) Tier 3: rewrite the LU factorization

B) No change: source stepping already does this

C) Tier 2: a continuation strategy plug-in behind the operating-point homotopy interface

D) Tier 1: set gmin
problems.a: Tier 2: a continuation strategy plug-in behind the operating-point homotopy interface
problems.e: Convergence strategies are policies. A seam for homotopy strategies lets a new one be added while the Newton kernel stays fixed.

problems.q:
An agent proposes a core edit to add a new device equation directly inside the matrix assembly loop. What should the harness steer it toward instead?

A) Adding the equation to the options card

B) Implementing the device behind the device-model interface as a plug-in

C) Hard-coding the device in every netlist

D) Accepting the edit if it compiles
problems.a: Implementing the device behind the device-model interface as a plug-in
problems.e: The same behavior fits at a lower tier. Keeping device equations out of the assembly loop keeps the core small and stable.

problems.q:
A pull request edits the Newton convergence test in the core. What verification should the harness require before a human reviews it?

A) No tests, since the change is small

B) The full golden regression suite and QoR comparison on reference decks

C) A compile-only check

D) One deck that previously failed
problems.a: The full golden regression suite and QoR comparison on reference decks
problems.e: A core change can alter results everywhere. The full golden suite and differential comparison show nothing unintended moved.

problems.q:
Requests to change the transient time loop keep arriving, each handled as a Tier 3 edit. What does that pattern indicate?

A) A seam is missing: the varying behavior should be moved behind an extension point

B) Tier 1 options should be removed

C) The core is well designed

D) The requests should be refused
problems.a: A seam is missing: the varying behavior should be moved behind an extension point
problems.e: A seam is in the right place when Tier 3 edits essentially never happen for that kind of change. Repeated core edits signal where one belongs.

label: Fast and accurate simulation in a sizing loop
prereqs: Table models and fast SPICE accuracy
Corners and Monte Carlo in circuit simulation
Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
lesson:
# Fast and accurate simulation in a sizing loop

Analog sizing loops evaluate thousands of candidate designs. An agent cannot afford accurate SPICE at every corner for every candidate, so it runs a fast simulator, a surrogate or a fast SPICE mode, to screen, and recurses into accurate SPICE only where the decision depends on it. Budgeting that loop, and knowing exactly which candidates the fast engine's error forces back to SPICE, turns the fast-and-accurate idea into numbers.

## Budgeting a two-level loop

A two-level loop screens $N$ candidates with a fast engine at $t_f$ per run and verifies the best $k$ in accurate SPICE at $C$ corners, $t_a$ per run. The total is $N t_f + k C t_a$. With 1000 candidates at 2 s, then the best 10 at 15 corners at 3 min, screening takes 33.3 min and verification 450 min, 483 min in all. Verification dominates, which is typical: corners multiply accurate cost. The budget tells an agent where to spend effort: a faster screen saves little here, while pruning corners per metric or verifying fewer candidates saves a lot. All runs are independent, so the wall time also divides by the available parallel licenses.

## Speedup over all-accurate

Running every candidate at every corner in accurate SPICE costs $N C t_a$. In the example, $1000 \times 15 \times 3 = 45000$ min against 483 min, a speedup of 93. The speedup is real only if the fast screen ranks candidates well enough that the true best design is among the $k$ verified. That requires the fast engine to be validated against SPICE golden results over the region the search explores. A surrogate trained on a different region can rank confidently and wrongly, and a reward computed from the fast engine alone invites an optimizer to exploit its errors, which is reward hacking against a proxy.

## Which candidates must be re-verified

A validated fast engine comes with an error bound $\pm e$. With a specification of gain at least $S$, a fast value above $S + e$ passes regardless of the error, a value below $S - e$ fails regardless, and a value within $[S - e, S + e]$ could go either way and must be re-simulated accurately. With $S = 70$ dB, $e = 1.5$ dB and fast gains 70.3, 67.5, 67.9, 66.9, 71.4, 68 and 73.9 dB, the band is 68.5 to 71.5 dB and two candidates fall in it. Tightening the fast engine's error bound shrinks the band and the accurate workload, which is the measurable payoff of better surrogates.

## Going deeper

Gielen and Rutenbar, "Computer-aided design of analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits" (Proceedings of the IEEE, 2000); Rutenbar, Gielen and Roychowdhury, "Hierarchical modeling, optimization, and synthesis for system-level analog and RF designs" (Proceedings of the IEEE, 2007).

problems.q: A sizing agent screens 200 candidate designs with a fast simulator at 2 s per run (one corner), then verifies the best 5 in accurate SPICE at 45 corners, 1 min per run. What is the total simulation time, in minutes? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Screening: $200 \times 2 / 60 = 6.67$ min. Verification: $5 \times 45 \times 1 = 225$ min. Total 231.67 min.

problems.q: A sizing agent screens 1000 candidate designs with a fast simulator at 2 s per run (one corner), then verifies the best 20 in accurate SPICE at 45 corners, 5 min per run. What is the total simulation time, in minutes? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Screening: $1000 \times 2 / 60 = 33.33$ min. Verification: $20 \times 45 \times 5 = 4500$ min. Total 4533.33 min.

problems.q: A sizing agent screens 1000 candidate designs with a fast simulator at 0.5 s per run (one corner), then verifies the best 20 in accurate SPICE at 9 corners, 1 min per run. What is the total simulation time, in minutes? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Screening: $1000 \times 0.5 / 60 = 8.33$ min. Verification: $20 \times 9 \times 1 = 180$ min. Total 188.33 min.

problems.q: A sizing agent screens 500 candidates with a fast simulator at 1 s per run, then verifies the best 5 in accurate SPICE at 9 corners, 1 min per run. Running every candidate at every corner in accurate SPICE instead would cost how many times as much? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: All-accurate: $500 \times 9 \times 1 = 4500$ min. Two-level: 53.33 min. Ratio 84.4.

problems.q: A sizing agent screens 2000 candidates with a fast simulator at 0.5 s per run, then verifies the best 20 in accurate SPICE at 15 corners, 2 min per run. Running every candidate at every corner in accurate SPICE instead would cost how many times as much? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: All-accurate: $2000 \times 15 \times 2 = 60000$ min. Two-level: 616.67 min. Ratio 97.3.

problems.q: A sizing agent screens 5000 candidates with a fast simulator at 6 s per run, then verifies the best 10 in accurate SPICE at 45 corners, 5 min per run. Running every candidate at every corner in accurate SPICE instead would cost how many times as much? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: All-accurate: $5000 \times 45 \times 5 = 1125000$ min. Two-level: 2750 min. Ratio 409.1.

problems.q: A fast simulator predicts gain within $\pm 1$ dB of SPICE, validated on a golden set. The spec is gain $\ge 70$ dB. Candidates whose fast gain clears the spec by more than the error bound are accepted, those below it by more than the bound are rejected, and the rest must be re-simulated accurately. The fast gains are 72.1, 70.6, 66, 68.2, 67.2, 71.2, 71.1, 68.2 dB. How many candidates must be re-simulated?
problems.e: Re-simulate every value within 1 dB of 70 dB, the band $[69, 71]$: 1 candidates. Outside the band the fast answer cannot flip the decision.

problems.q: A fast simulator predicts gain within $\pm 1$ dB of SPICE, validated on a golden set. The spec is gain $\ge 65$ dB. Candidates whose fast gain clears the spec by more than the error bound are accepted, those below it by more than the bound are rejected, and the rest must be re-simulated accurately. The fast gains are 61, 62.3, 68, 68.6, 63.7, 67.8, 68.1, 66.1, 66.1 dB. How many candidates must be re-simulated?
problems.e: Re-simulate every value within 1 dB of 65 dB, the band $[64, 66]$: 0 candidates. Outside the band the fast answer cannot flip the decision.

problems.q: A fast simulator predicts gain within $\pm 2$ dB of SPICE, validated on a golden set. The spec is gain $\ge 70$ dB. Candidates whose fast gain clears the spec by more than the error bound are accepted, those below it by more than the bound are rejected, and the rest must be re-simulated accurately. The fast gains are 67.8, 67.5, 66.9, 70, 66, 73.7, 73.6 dB. How many candidates must be re-simulated?
problems.e: Re-simulate every value within 2 dB of 70 dB, the band $[68, 72]$: 1 candidates. Outside the band the fast answer cannot flip the decision.

label: Verifying a surrogate against SPICE
prereqs: Corners and Monte Carlo in circuit simulation
lesson:
# Verifying a surrogate against SPICE

ML surrogates promise SPICE-like answers in microseconds: cell delays, amplifier gains, waveform features. Before an agent may use one in a loop, the surrogate must be verified against SPICE golden results with checkable acceptance rules. The metrics differ in what they reveal: a worst-case error bounds decisions, a failure count maps where the surrogate cannot be trusted, and an RMS error summarizes typical accuracy.

## Worst-case relative error

For each golden point with SPICE value $g$ and surrogate value $s$, the relative error is $|s - g|/|g|$. The worst case over the golden set is the number a decision can rely on. For pairs (238, 228), (87, 95) and (232, 244) ps, the errors are 4.2%, 9.2% and 5.2%, so the worst is 9.2%, set by the shortest delay, where a fixed absolute error is a larger fraction. Worst-case error is only as good as the golden set's coverage: points must span the input space the agent will query, including corners and extreme loads, or the bound says nothing about the region that matters.

## Counting tolerance failures

An acceptance rule such as "at most 3% relative error per point" turns verification into a count. Each failing point marks a region where the surrogate must not be used and the agent must fall back to SPICE, or where more training data is needed. For pairs (164, 166), (58, 70), (101, 107), (273, 263), (71, 66) and (193, 184) ps, the errors are 1.2%, 20.7%, 5.9%, 3.7%, 7.0% and 4.7%, so five of six fail. That surrogate is unusable at this tolerance, whatever its average. Failure locations matter more than the count: clusters at small delays or extreme inputs reveal systematic weaknesses rather than noise.

## RMS error over the golden set

The RMS error $\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n}\sum (s_i - g_i)^2}$ summarizes typical accuracy in the metric's own unit. For differences of $-5, -1, 1, -10, -12$ and 4 ps, the mean square is $287/6 = 47.8$ ps$^2$ and the RMS error is 6.92 ps. RMS is what training minimizes, which is why a surrogate can look good on it while failing the worst-case or per-point rules: a few large errors hide among many small ones. A verification gate for an agent's surrogate should therefore combine metrics, and it should be rerun as a differential check whenever the surrogate or the SPICE models it imitates change.

## Going deeper

Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, "The Elements of Statistical Learning" (2nd ed., Springer, 2009), on model assessment; the ngspice manual, on .measure for generating golden metrics.

problems.q: An ML surrogate predicts cell delays and is checked against SPICE golden results. The pairs (SPICE, surrogate), in ps, are: (286, 296), (73, 70), (266, 257), (102, 111), (248, 243). What is the worst-case relative error, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Relative error is $|s - g|/g$. The worst is the pair (102, 111): 8.82%. A worst-case bound, not an average, is what a sign-off decision can rely on.

label: The device-model seam
prereqs: Linearizing a MOSFET at a Newton iterate
lesson:
# The device-model seam

The device-model interface is the simulator's most important seam. The core asks one question per device per iteration: given these terminal voltages, temperature and parameters, what are the currents, charges and their derivatives? Everything model-specific lives behind that question. Designing the seam well, and testing what passes through it, is what lets new transistor models arrive as plug-ins instead of core edits.

## What the device interface returns

For each device the core supplies terminal voltages, temperature, instance parameters and the analysis mode. The model returns terminal currents, which form the Newton residual; their derivatives with respect to terminal voltages, which form the Jacobian; terminal charges, which the integrator differentiates so that charge is conserved; charge derivatives, the capacitances used in transient and AC; and, in noise analysis, its noise source densities. A MOSFET returning $g_m$, $g_{ds}$ and $I_{eq}$ at an iterate is exactly this contract. A narrow, stable interface like this lets the core treat a diode and a BSIM transistor identically, as stamps.

## Adding a model as a plug-in

A new model, typically written in Verilog-A, is compiled into code that implements the device interface and loads at run time, leaving the solver untouched: a Tier 2 change. Good plug-ins follow the seam rules: no hidden global state, so results are deterministic and order-independent; a frozen extension ABI, so compiled models survive simulator releases; and coarse calls, evaluating many instances of one model per call. A plug-in whose currents are right but whose derivatives have a sign error still converges to the right answer, because the residual uses the currents, but Newton slows or fails, which is why derivative correctness is a separate test.

## Testing a new device model

Device-level tests check the interface contract: compare the returned Jacobian with finite differences of the returned currents at many bias points; check continuity and source-drain symmetry near $V_{DS} = 0$, where many models kink and cause convergence failures and wrong distortion; and, for a speed-optimized rewrite, compare currents, charges and derivatives with the reference model over a grid of biases and temperatures. Circuit-level golden tests then catch what device tests miss, such as charge errors: if a ring oscillator built from the model runs 5% faster than its golden result, promotion is blocked, and the golden value is not updated to match.

## Going deeper

McAndrew et al., "Best practices for compact modeling in Verilog-A" (IEEE Journal of the Electron Devices Society, 2015); the Xyce Users' Guide, on device models.

problems.q:
Why should the device interface also return noise sources?

A) To set gmin

B) To randomize the transient

C) Noise analysis needs each device's noise power densities to propagate them to the output

D) To report Monte Carlo statistics
problems.a: Noise analysis needs each device's noise power densities to propagate them to the output
problems.e: Noise analysis sums device noise through transfer functions, so each model reports its thermal, shot and flicker densities at the operating point.

problems.q:
At each Newton iteration the simulator calls a device model through its interface. What must the model return?

A) The full MNA matrix

B) Terminal currents and charges, and their derivatives with respect to the terminal voltages

C) Only the terminal currents

D) The next timestep
problems.a: Terminal currents and charges, and their derivatives with respect to the terminal voltages
problems.e: The core stamps currents into the residual and the derivatives (conductances and capacitances) into the Jacobian. Charges serve transient and AC.

problems.q:
Which context should a device-model seam expose to the model, beyond terminal voltages?

A) Temperature, instance parameters and the analysis mode, such as DC, transient, AC or noise

B) The other devices' internal state

C) The plotting settings

D) The full netlist text
problems.a: Temperature, instance parameters and the analysis mode, such as DC, transient, AC or noise
problems.e: Models depend on temperature and geometry and must provide extra data in some analyses, such as noise sources in noise analysis.

problems.q:
A team writes a new transistor model in Verilog-A. How does it typically reach a SPICE-class simulator without editing the simulator core?

A) It replaces the LU solver

B) It is converted to a .options card

C) A Verilog-A compiler generates code that loads through the simulator's model interface

D) It is pasted into the Newton loop
problems.a: A Verilog-A compiler generates code that loads through the simulator's model interface
problems.e: Compiled Verilog-A plug-ins, for example through standardized compiled-model interfaces, implement the device seam while the core stays fixed.

problems.q:
A plug-in model keeps a static counter that changes its output on every call. What rule of good seams does this break?

A) Coarse calls

B) Narrow interfaces

C) A frozen ABI

D) No hidden global state: results must be deterministic for the same inputs
problems.a: No hidden global state: results must be deterministic for the same inputs
problems.e: Hidden state makes results depend on call order, so repeated runs and differential tests stop being reproducible.

problems.q:
A team writes a new transistor model in Verilog-A. How does it typically reach a SPICE-class simulator without editing the simulator core?

A) It replaces the LU solver

B) It is pasted into the Newton loop

C) A Verilog-A compiler generates code that loads through the simulator's model interface

D) It is converted to a .options card
problems.a: A Verilog-A compiler generates code that loads through the simulator's model interface
problems.e: Compiled Verilog-A plug-ins, for example through standardized compiled-model interfaces, implement the device seam while the core stays fixed.

problems.q:
A plug-in model shows a discontinuity in drain current at Vds = 0 when tested. Why test that point specifically?

A) It tests the timestep control

B) Vds = 0 is never simulated

C) Symmetry and continuity at Vds = 0 are where many models fail, causing Newton and distortion problems

D) It is the only point with nonzero current
problems.a: Symmetry and continuity at Vds = 0 are where many models fail, causing Newton and distortion problems
problems.e: Source-drain symmetry tests near Vds = 0 are standard model quality checks, because kinks there cause convergence failures and wrong harmonic distortion.

problems.q:
A model passes its device-level tests, but a ring oscillator built from it runs 5% faster than the golden result. What should happen?

A) Block promotion and investigate, since circuit-level golden tests disagree

B) Promote it, since device tests passed

C) Loosen the tolerance to 6%

D) Update the golden result to match
problems.a: Block promotion and investigate, since circuit-level golden tests disagree
problems.e: Golden circuit tests catch interactions device tests miss, such as charge errors. A failed golden check blocks promotion.

problems.q:
A new model is meant to reproduce an existing one with a speed optimization. What does the differential test compare?

A) Only compile time

B) The source line count

C) The number of parameters

D) Currents, charges and derivatives from both models over a grid of biases and temperatures, plus golden circuit results
problems.a: Currents, charges and derivatives from both models over a grid of biases and temperatures, plus golden circuit results
problems.e: A differential test proves the optimization changed nothing beyond a numerical tolerance, at the device and the circuit level.
